Second, approximate the full evolution operator using a Lie-Trotter-Suzuki (LTS) decomposition of the desired approximation order in time step. The I-LTS construction ensures that the full evolution operator can be represented as a product of terms that each have an efficient explicit tensor product factorization that can be handled efficiently with tensor network and/or quantum block-encoding methods. Next, we apply this method to an important non-integrable point example of a dynamical system: the Stepanoff flow on the torus. First, we derive an efficient unitary quantum algorithm for simulating the Stepanoff flow that can be thought of as a unitary classical version of a quantum map. Then, we provide a detailed description of the encoding of the two-dimensional system into an efficient quantum circuit, including an efficient block-encoding for all required operators. An efficient Hamiltonian simulation algorithm is constructed using a sequence of alternating quantum Fourier transforms (QFT) and Quantum Signal Processing (QSP) circuits. Finally, the circuit is simulated using a numerical emulator of fault-tolerant quantum computers, and the results are found to be consistent with several alternative classical computational methods. While efficient, the need for Trotterization introduces fundamental complexity in requiring small enough time step for an accurate approximation and solving for the transfer operator requires one to confront the linear scaling of the advection operator with grid size.

papers.title: When to Trust a PFN: Detecting Harmful Shift in Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Tabular prior-fitted networks (PFNs) work well across tabular classification problems but can fail silently at deployment when distributions shift. We propose CALD (Calibrated Anchor-Loss Disagreement), a lightweight unsupervised monitor that triggers an alarm to warn when a PFN might fail. By finetuning the decoder to maximize disagreement with the test-set prediction while maintaining accuracy on an ID anchor set, CALD identifies harmful OOD batches through the resulting anchor loss, requiring no labels on test batches. We prove that the post-finetune anchor loss has a strictly lower expectation under sufficiently severe shift than under ID eval, yielding a one-sided test. Across 14 datasets covering tabular and structured distribution shift, on both TabPFN and TabICL, CALD matches or outperforms baselines on harmful shifts and is markedly more resilient to benign-shift false alarms.

papers.title: Plasma transport by carrier electrons: Nernst advection beyond the heat-flow analogy due to kinetic stress
papers.abstract: Nernst advection of magnetic fields down temperature gradients is lowered by kinetic stress from the $\underline{\underline{f}}_2$ electron distribution harmonic, which allows fluxes to stream past one another without isotropizing their lateral momentum. The long-held tie between heat-flow and Nernst advection is disrupted. When the distance between electron collisions is comparable to the magnetic field length-scale $L_B$, the kinetic stress affects magnetic transport in plasmas otherwise regarded as classical. This is from carrier electrons being deflected back and forth over the course of their trajectory. The field structure Knudsen number is defined: $Kn_B=14.8\frac{\lambda_{ei}}{L_B}\frac{Z+0.40}{Z+4.86}$, with Nernst velocity halved by kinetic effects at $Kn_B=1$. The kinetic stress is relocalized by magnetization, following the relocalization of heat-flux. Righi-Leduc heat-flow is found to be similarly suppressed by kinetic stress. The linear results of this paper are found to faithfully represent the non-linear evolution of magnetic field at a heat-front, indicating that low-$Z$ plasmas throughout magnetized-HED are demagnetized more slowly than previously anticipated.

papers.title: The positive-sphere variant of Tingley's problem for $C^1([0,1])$
papers.abstract: Let $C^1([0,1])$ be endowed with the norm $\|f\|=\|f\|_\infty+\|f'\|_\infty$, and let $S(C^1([0,1]))^+$ be the part of its unit sphere consisting of nonnegative, nondecreasing functions. We prove that every surjective isometry of $S(C^1([0,1]))^+$ is the identity and has a unique surjective real-linear isometric extension to $C^1([0,1])$.

papers.title: Anytime-Valid Sequential Verification for Sensing-Efficient Robot Navigation under Perception Uncertainty
papers.abstract: When a robot navigates an unfamiliar grid, noisy sensor readings can make it hard to tell whether the cells along its next move are free. Additional scans can reduce that uncertainty, but a fixed scan count spends the same sensing effort at every position. In a static-grid simulation, a sequential rule uses a Gaussian likelihood ratio to determine when the cells newly covered by the robot's footprint have enough evidence of free space. On 324 held-out scenarios from 18 public maps, the sequential gate and a four-scan reference chosen on validation data both completed every mission without an observed collision. With their respective validation-selected routing weights, the gate averaged 123.15 scans per episode versus 224.13 for the reference, a reduction of 45.05% (95% map-stratified bootstrap interval: 42.21--48.95%). In a retrospective check on the same scenarios with routing weights held equal, the reductions were 43.91% and 43.37% at the two tested weights, with all missions completed. On 216 scenarios from 12 previously unused maps, allocating more of the same certification error budget near the initial start--goal rectangle cut the sequential gate's scan count by a further 11.58%. The spatial variant completed 206 missions versus 208 for the original gate and increased computation time. The collision bound depends on the assumed observation model and footprint geometry. In a stress test with persistent per-cell bias, the original gate completed 0 of 54 missions.

papers.title: InterConRank: Joint Node Centrality in Interconnected Heterogeneous Networks
papers.abstract: Two nodes with identical connections within their own layer can differ in importance if their neighbors in another layer occupy different positions in the network. We introduce InterConRank, a centrality algorithm that computes a separate node ranking for each layer of an interconnected network. Directed dependencies specify which layers supply scores to each receiving layer. InterConRank normalizes each type of link separately and updates all layers together, so a score can cross into a layer in one iteration and propagate along its internal links in the next. We prove convergence of this joint update and evaluate the resulting rankings on four scholarly networks. On all four networks, InterConRank gives the highest rank correlations with both h-index and total citations for nodes in the collaboration layer.

papers.title: TASK Memory: Beyond Text-Only Memory with Activation Steering and Knowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on external memory, yet they still hallucinate about what they remember. Often the correct memory is retrieved and placed in the prompt, but the answer contradicts it or the memory is applied to the wrong question. We call these use-time memory hallucinations. Across five open models, we find that they arise from the conflict between parametric knowledge and external memory and take three forms: memory-ignoring, where the model returns to a stale fact in its weights (up to 46% of queries); memory-misapplying, where it attributes the memory to unrelated entities (up to 24%, and 49% when retrieval is combined with weight editing); and version confusion, where 53% of answers about revised facts assert the superseded value when both versions remain stored. We propose TASK memory, which goes beyond text-only memory by combining a Text note with Activation Steering and Knowledge editing that share one in-model address. The text holds the content. A removable knowledge edit supplies the address through its subject key and supports multi-hop composition. A pair of steering vectors decides, query by query, whether the model adopts the memory or keeps its own answer; the vectors store no content and control how the text memory is used. On frozen models under a pre-registered, test-once protocol, TASK reduces memory-ignoring hallucinations to at most 1.5% in all ten model-dataset cells and cuts neighbour misuse from 39.2% to 7.5% (+10.8 pp composite on CounterFact). It improves a 300-memory library over BM25 RAG by 16.4 pp, an advantage that holds at 3,000 memories, resolves fact revisions without fact IDs, and adds 7.5 pp of multi-hop accuracy on MQuAKE. 21 of 23 cross-model comparisons (8B-27B, four families) are significant, and TASK beats three recent context-steering methods in 9 of 10 model-dataset cells.

papers.title: Time-optimal travel driven by two vector fields on a Riemannian manifold
papers.abstract: We study minimum-time travel on a Riemannian manifold $(M,h)$ for a kinematic model in which finitely many drift fields contribute additively to the velocity, after independent rescaling of their components parallel and orthogonal to a chosen unit direction $u$. The velocity is then $\mathcal Y_x(u)=(\eta(x)+h_x(\widehat Z_x,u))u+\widehat W_x$, $u\in UT_xM$, for two effective vector fields $\widehat Z$, $\widehat W$ and a self-propulsion speed $\eta\geq0$. Let $F$ be the gauge of the radial hull $\mathcal B_x=[0,1]\cdot\mathcal S_x$ of the velocity set $\mathcal S_x=\mathcal Y_x(UT_xM)$. Where $\eta>0$, we characterize when $F$ is a Finsler metric and give two-sided estimates and representation formulae for it; where $\eta=0$ and $\widehat Z\neq0$, we recover the Randers, Kropina and strong-wind regimes of Zermelo navigation. Examples include Matsumoto's slope metric, traction-modified slope models, and alternative models for wildfire propagation and microswimmer navigation. Since $F$ need not be a Finsler metric, we treat the minimum-time problem with tools from differential inclusions. For distinct endpoints, the inclusions defined by $\mathcal S_x$ and $\mathcal B_x$ give the same infimum travel time, and so does the convex hull of $\mathcal B_x$ under local controllability at the terminal point. When $F$ is finite, the infimum is attained if $(M,h)$ is complete, $\mathcal Y$ is bounded and each $\mathcal B_x$ is convex. When $F$ is a Finsler metric on $\{\eta>0\}$, the set $\{\eta=0\}$ cannot be reached from $\{\eta>0\}$ in finite time and, on $\{\eta>0\}$, the minimum time is the Finsler distance; if moreover $(M,h)$ is complete and $\eta$ is bounded, $F$ is forward and backward complete and the minimum time is attained by geodesics. We also compute the support Hamiltonian directly from the velocity law, for every $\eta\geq0$.

papers.title: One Model, Many Modes: Evolving System Prompt Ensembles for Creative Generation
papers.abstract: Preference-aligned LLMs can exhibit mode collapse, concentrating their output distributions around a narrow set of high-reward responses. This limits creative generation, which requires quality, novelty, and diversity. Existing test-time methods often emphasize diversity, giving less attention to whether individual responses are both high-quality and novel. This distinction matters in practical use, where users may seek a single compelling, original response. We formalize creative generation as a multi-objective distributional optimization problem and introduce SEPO, a training-free framework for System Prompt Ensemble Optimization. The framework combines prompt evolution with greedy max-min selection to identify behaviorally distinct system prompts under a quality constraint, then uniformly samples one prompt per response at inference time. Across four creative generation tasks with increasing quality requirements and three open-weight models, SEPO ranks first in 8 of 12 settings on the harmonic mean of quality, diversity, and novelty, while no baseline leads in more than two. On average, it raises LLM-judged diversity from 1.92 to 3.43 and novelty from 1.00 to 3.34 over base sampling (1-5 scale), with quality decreasing from 3.72 to 3.30. We further show that expanding the optimized ensemble increases separation among prompt-conditioned response distributions. These results support system prompt ensemble optimization as a promising approach to improving LLM creativity at inference time.

papers.title: Minimizing Optical Circuit Reconfigurations for Concurrent Collectives
papers.abstract: Optical circuit switches (OCSes) provide high-bandwidth point-to-point circuits in GPU clusters, but each optical port attaches to only one peer at a time, and reconfiguring a connection interrupts transmission. In large-model training, these ports are shared by many communication domains, each running its own collective instance, called a CCL kernel; often, several of these kernels execute the same collective at the same time. Because each step of the collective can reach a different peer, domains advancing through the steps in the same order may require a reconfiguration at every step. We introduce the mega CCL kernel to schedule these kernels jointly. When a collective permits its steps to be reordered, different domains can take different legal steps in the same round, letting consecutive rounds share the same circuits and reducing the number of reconfigurations. Because the kernels are interchangeable, we need not decide the steps of every kernel separately. Instead, in each round we count how many kernels run each pattern, and then use bipartite matching to turn those counts into a concrete schedule for each kernel. We call this the count model, as opposed to the direct formulation that decides each kernel separately, and prove that the two give the same configuration sequences and the same optimum while the count model is substantially easier to solve. On a fully loaded 64-supernode, 64-domain scheduling instance, joint scheduling cuts pairwise-AlltoAll reconfigurations from 62 to 3 and HD AllReduce from 10 to 2. In synthetic training replays parameterized by eight real models, it reduces iteration time by up to about 34%; on a 64-GPU test case, the count model solves over six orders of magnitude faster than the direct formulation.

papers.title: Reading Fine-Tuning Diffs Through Lenses: Model Diffing for Backdoor Detection
papers.abstract: We introduce a common scoring system based on token readouts to evaluate weight, activation and output-based model diffing methods for backdoor detection in fine-tuning processes. We also improve existing weight and activation based methods by incorporating the $J$-lens and its refinement, the $J{+}{+}$-lens. We test our setup in experiments where we compare a backdoored model with the base model from which it was fine-tuned. Our results show that incorporating the $J{+}{+}$-lens improves the weight-based method in all our settings, while the $J$-lens improves its ranks within single layers. The strongest single method is $\Delta W J{+}{+}$, the weight difference decoded through the $J{+}{+}$-lens of the base model, which ranks a token naming the backdoor among its first ten tokens in 11 of our 12 settings. Moreover, we show that output and activation based methods such as ADL and Diff Mining can easily break if the backdoored model is penalised during fine-tuning for giving the backdoor's words probability on clean inputs, whereas the weight-based methods are not affected. Conversely, permuting the hidden units or training only the layers that read the residual stream hides the backdoor from the weight-based methods but not from ADL and Diff Mining. No single method resists both attacks.

papers.title: On the Convergence of Discrete-Time Primal-Dual Algorithm for Distributed GNE Seeking
papers.abstract: We investigate the convergence of a discrete-time distributed primal-dual algorithm for generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) seeking in a class of noncooperative games with nonlinear coupling constraints. We establish semi-global convergence of the algorithm under a fixed stepsize, in the sense that convergence can be guaranteed from any prescribed compact set of initial conditions by choosing a sufficiently small stepsize. Under a diminishing stepsize sequence, we further establish global convergence when the constraints are globally Lipschitz continuous. For the special case of affine constraints, global convergence is also guaranteed under a sufficiently small fixed stepsize. Finally, we extend these convergence results to a fully distributed GNE seeking algorithm in a partial-decision information setting, where each agent only has access to the actions of its neighbors. These results complement existing convergence results for continuous-time primal-dual dynamics, and provide new convergence guarantees for the discrete-time counterpart in distributed GNE seeking.

papers.title: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: Fully online on-policy distillation (OPD) is costly for long-horizon agents because each update depends on fresh environment rollouts. Prefix replay offers an efficient alternative by sampling current-student responses from stored histories, reducing idle time for long-tail rollouts and allowing each collected trajectory to support multiple updates. However, our analysis of the complete prefix replay pipeline identifies two limitations in long-horizon settings. In trajectory collection, teacher-only trajectories miss student-induced histories, while broader history coverage can reduce teacher reliability. In trajectory reuse, fixed position-based schedules cannot identify critical decisions that may occur at any trajectory depth. We introduce CARE-OPD (Collect for coverAge, Replay with Evidence) to address both limitations. Student-seeded teacher completions and response-level confidence gating expand history coverage while filtering unreliable updates. Hindsight replay allocation then uses downstream execution evidence to select consequential turns. Across long-horizon tasks Software Engineering and Deep Research, CARE-OPD outperforms online OPD and prior prefix replay baselines. On SWE-bench Verified, it raises task success to 59.5% while reducing end-to-end training time by 45% and environment actions by 44% relative to asynchronous online OPD.

papers.title: Fewer Parameters, Longer Runtimes: The Wall-Clock Cost of Hybrid Quantum Physics-Informed Neural Networks
papers.abstract: While hybrid quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks (QCPINNs) are often described as efficient because they have fewer trainable parameters than classical PINNs, parameter count does not measure wall-clock cost. To examine this gap on a one-dimensional seawater temperature diffusion benchmark, with the quantum circuits simulated on a CPU, we time the four cumulative stages a PINN needs (the forward pass, the first- and second-order input gradients, and the PDE-loss parameter gradient) for a classical PINN, four hybrid configurations that differ in qubit count and circuit depth, and size-matched classical controls that share the hybrids' classical layers. We find that the hybrids are 14-56x slower than the classical PINN for the forward pass and 10-97x slower for the PDE-loss parameter gradient, and even against the size-matched controls, they remain 9-85x slower. Further, over the tested ranges, runtime increased approximately exponentially with qubit count, approximately linearly with circuit depth, and sub-linearly with batch size, while for the circuit-only forward pass, a second simulator backend was 10-165x slower under the same calling pattern. Although the hybrids have 38-44% fewer parameters than the classical PINN, this reduction comes from their smaller classical layers, as the quantum circuit accounts for at most 2.5% of each hybrid's parameters. Yet parameter count failed to predict runtime even among the classical networks, since the size-matched controls, despite having fewer parameters than the classical PINN, run slower than it. Our conclusion is that fewer parameters did not mean lower cost: every hybrid took at least ten times longer than the classical PINN at every stage, and the gap grew quickly with the number of qubits.

papers.title: AutoRSP: An AI Agent for Radar Sensing Pipeline Design
papers.abstract: Radar sensing demands a pipeline that is well-thought-out across hardware and software. We ask whether an AI agent can automatically design radar sensing pipelines at a fraction of the time, cost, and expertise that current practice needs. We present AutoRSP, an agent that embeds radar-system-level structure through sub-agents mapped to five stack layers, a code-based representation of every layer with explicitly modeled cross-layer dependencies. Feedback for the agentic search process comes from a pipeline of realistic RF simulation, on-sensor emulation, and execution on real edge devices, rather than from an LLM judge. Because such feedback can be slower than an LLM call, we present methods to efficiently optimize agentic loops. We evaluate AutoRSP on robotic imaging, automotive perception, and vital sign sensing. It produces executable pipelines with performance comparable to or better than human-expert pipelines and closed-source agents. AutoRSP's harness, tools, and benchmarks will be released to bridge the rising gap in agentic research abilities outside of frontier labs.

papers.title: periapsis: A Comprehensive Orbital Fitting Package
papers.abstract: We introduce a new Python package \texttt{periapsis}, which computes posterior distributions for a variety of orbital parameters given astrometric and/or radial velocity data. \texttt{periapsis} not only returns posterior distributions, but also a variety of statistics assessing convergence and fit metrics as well as plotting capabilities for visualizing the orbital systems. In this paper, we describe our various methods for fitting Keplerian orbits to both astrometric and radial velocity data. We then show the breadth of binary systems that \texttt{periapsis} can characterize by comparing our computed parameters with known orbital systems. Finally, we discuss how \texttt{periapsis} will be a helpful tool for future data releases like \textit{Gaia} DR4 and \textit{Roman}.

papers.title: Microscopic Approach to Neutron Elastic and Inelastic Cross Sections
papers.abstract: Depending on the nuclei involved and the beam energies, reaction timescales differ tremendously. Today, distinct models are often used to describe each timescale, relying on phenomenological inputs, such as level densities or partial-widths, which limits their predictive power. This work aims to address this issue by providing a unified description of low-energy neutron elastic and inelastic reaction channels starting from microscopic predictions of the structure of mid-mass nuclei. The goal is to build a framework that is general enough to span the different reaction regimes while remaining anchored in microscopic theory. For illustration purposes, this work focuses on reactions $n+^{20}$Ne to the elastic and inelastic channels. The S-matrix is build from shell model predictions of resonances states and their spectroscopic amplitudes for $^{21}$Ne, using two different approximations of the single-particle asymptotics. Then, the shell-model predictions for the level density and single-particle partial widths are analyzed and the final cross sections are compared with evaluated ones. This method qualitatively reproduces the ENDF evaluation for the $^{20}$Ne$(n,el)$ and $^{20}$Ne$(n,n')$ cross sections. The present study also compares the Shannon entropy obtained from this model to the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE). In the future, the framework will be extended to include more complex reaction channels, such as two-nucleon and gamma channels, enabling more accurate predictions of neutron-induced reactions such as those of astrophysical interest.

papers.title: What Is a Theory Worth to an LLM Solver? Measuring, Inducing, and Merging Theories in Context
papers.abstract: Mathematicians solve problems faster when they know the right theory. We ask how much a stated theory is worth to a large language model (LLM) solver, and whether a model can write that theory itself. In a length-matched protocol, adding the right theory to the context of Qwen3-14B raises pass@1 on pattern waiting-time problems from 0.37 to 0.83 and cuts the median tokens of correct solutions from 10.2k to 6.3k, while worked examples of the same length do not help. The gain shrinks as the solver and its token budget grow (+0.46, +0.26, +0.07), and at a long budget it comes almost entirely from finishing within budget: solutions that finish are correct 98--100\% of the time in every condition. To separate induction from recall, we plant unpublished theorems in custom probability families and measure how much of the oracle theory's gain an induced theory recovers. A strong open model, required to explore the training problems with code before writing, recovers 60\% of the gain on one planted family, 48\% on a second, and almost none on a third, where it finds the right form but not the condition that makes the form computable. No single induced note is complete, but a strong model that merges several notes recovers 61\% of the gain on the classic family, above the best single note (47\%). Theories are worth the reasoning they save, and models can find their pieces before they can assemble them.

papers.title: SOLVE: Sparse, Ordered Keyposes Make LLM Agents Versatile and Efficient Robot Manipulator
papers.abstract: LLM agents have made remarkable progress in robot manipulation, yet they suffer from expensive inference, dense step-by-step control, and tool bottlenecks. We introduce SOLVE, a training-free, versatile and efficient agent policy: a multimodal LLM agent writes a sparse, ordered sequence of 6-DoF end-effector keyposes per call, observes the result, and writes the next, while a motion planner interpolates between them. The agent decides the number and spacing of keyposes for both fast long-range motion and fine-grained manipulation. This granularity matches the sparsity of teleoperated manipulation: most demonstrations in DROID can be compressed into a few keyposes instead of dense actions. SOLVE grounds keyposes with sparse depth queries answered by noisy sources, such as multi-view triangulation, stereo, or monocular depth, and copes with that noise itself. It also improves from execution feedback, reflecting on its own rollouts and distilling a few rules per task. SOLVE reaches state-of-the-art performance of 74.5% on RoboDojo and 84.5% on RoboLab, with only $1.7 per episode on average, 12x less than previous dense-control agent policies. On a real robot, the same agent achieves an 88% success rate (75 of 85 episodes) over 16 challenging zero-shot tasks. Our project page is at https://serenos.github.io/solve-website.

papers.title: Weitzenbeock's theorem in arbitrary characteristic
papers.abstract: Let \(k\) be a field and \(V\) a finite-dimensional rational representation of the additive group \(\GG_{a,k}\). We show that the ring of invariants \(k[V]^{\GG_a}\) is finitely generated in every characteristic, extending Weitzenb\"ock's classical theorem beyond characteristic zero.

papers.title: The truncated $\mathbb{Z}-$moment problem
papers.abstract: We study the truncated moment problem on the one-dimensional full integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}$, seeking necessary and sufficient conditions for a prescribed sequence of $n$ real numbers to be $\mathbb{Z}-$representable, i.e. to be the sequence of the first $n$ moments of a probability measure supported on $\mathbb{Z}$. Building on the approach developed in 2017 in Infusino et al. for the truncated moment problem on the non-negative integers, we establish a complete characterization of $\mathbb{Z}-$representable sequences for every truncation order $n$. From this result, we derive an inductive and computable $\mathbb{Z}-$representability criterion. More generally, we also investigate the relationship between the truncated $\mathbb{Z}-$moment problem and the truncated Hamburger moment problem, seen as its continuous counterpart.

papers.title: phenjax: the IMRPhenomT waveform family in JAX for accelerated analyses on CPUs and GPUs
papers.abstract: We present phenjax, a JAX implementation of the precessing time-domain IMRPhenomT family of models for the gravitational wave signal emitted in compact binary coalescence. The code keeps the structure of its reference Python implementation, phenomxpy, and reproduces, on average, its polarizations to a few $\times 10^{-12}$ of the peak strain for all the models, aligned-spin and precessing. The waveform models now take advantage of the JAX construction: compiled once per array shape, vectorized over events (batching), differentiable and executed on CPUs or GPUs with the same source code. Different additional features address the cost of long signals and of heterogeneous populations in a batch. On one NVIDIA H100, for the precessing TPHM model on LISA-mass populations, phenjax is 3 to 6 times faster than phenomxpy when both codes evaluate one event at a time and 20 to 30 times faster when phenjax evaluates the events in batches of 8. We estimate that, for waveform generation, one GPU does the work of 1300 to 2700 cores of a current CPU node at 25 to 45 times less energy per waveform. As a backend of a global-fit LISA massive black hole pipeline, performed on the Sangria dataset, phenjax recovers the same posteriors as the other waveform backends at a lower computational cost. In a comparison with phentax, the wall time was 13 minutes instead of 21.

papers.title: BRIAR: Martingale Belief Smoothing on Bifurcation-Guided Reasoning Trees
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has rapidly advanced long-chain reasoning, yet standard policy optimizers distribute rollout compute and gradient credit blindly across a trajectory. On hard problems, an early misstep derails the remaining trace, whereas on solvable problems, the policy keeps generating redundant verification long after the answer is already determined. We trace both pathologies to a single structural fact: under an on-policy verifier, the true prefix pass probability $V^\pi(u)$ along a reasoning trace forms a $[0,1]$-bounded Doob martingale whose learnable credit variance is strictly conserved and bounded above by $V^\pi(u)(1-V^\pi(u))$, vanishing at both the derailed ($V^\pi\to 0$) and absorbed ($V^\pi\to 1$) boundaries. We introduce BRIAR (Bifurcation-guided Rollout and Inference on Adaptive Reasoning trees), a tree-structured RLVR framework built directly around this martingale geometry. First, BRIAR expands discourse-aligned reasoning trees along an upper-confidence outcome-bifurcation frontier, steering rollouts away from absorbed rumination and toward unresolved decision points. Second, it models latent node values with boundary-scaled heteroscedastic edge variances and computes exact global posteriors in linear $\mathcal{O}(|V|)$ time via two-pass Rauch--Tung--Striebel (RTS) tree belief smoothing, eliminating $\mathcal{O}(m^3)$ matrix inversions while gating out spurious boundary noise. Third, BRIAR detects minimal absorbed frontier nodes and applies zero-sum log-length centered suffix advantages strictly post-absorption, leaving pre-absorption derivations provably invariant.

papers.title: How Well Do Vision-Language Scene Graphs Serve as Memory for Embodied Question Answering?
papers.abstract: Embodied QA needs memory, but answer accuracy mixes retained evidence, reading errors and question priors. For a simulated multi-room scene-graph pipeline we define answerability: the fraction of questions a fixed rule-based reader answers correctly from the graph alone. The baseline recovers 24.1% of visible object types and its room labels flicker. Four targeted repairs double recall, raise answerability from 27.2% to 37.4%, and improve retrained QA from 71.4% to 75.9%, yet better object F1 can lower answerability. A question-type prior beats this reader on every predicted graph. In one real-video test, graph memory lowers accuracy. These exploratory findings favour scoring retained evidence alongside accuracy.

papers.title: Prevalence of the periodicity of maximizing measures
papers.abstract: For a continuous map $T\colon X\rightarrow X$ on a compact metric space $(X,d)$, we say that a function $f\colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ has the property $\mathscr{P}_T$ if its time averages along forward orbits of $T$ are maximized at a periodic orbit. In this article, we establish the Hunt--Ott conjecture (cf.~\cite{HO96a,HO96b}), that is, the property $\mathscr{P}_T$ is prevalent (in the sense of Hunt--Sauer--Yorke) in the space of Lipschitz functions with respect to a standard metric for subshifts of finite type. This result is a strengthening of \cite[Theorem~A]{BZ16} and \cite[Theorem~1.1]{DLZ24}, confirms the prediction mentioned in the ICM proceeding contribution of Bochi (\cite[Section~1]{Boc18}) suggested by experimental evidence.

papers.title: Black holes in little red and blue dots drive no superwinds in the first 1.5 billion years
papers.abstract: Galaxy-formation models rely on accreting black holes to expel gas from their hosts. We test this prediction in 67 little red dots (LRDs) and little blue dots (LBDs) in the first 1.5 billion years, selected from 80,367 NIRSpec spectra in the DAWN JWST Archive. We detect no [O III] wind, against lower limits of 7.2 and 7.5 expected detections for local sub-Eddington and super-Eddington active nuclei. For winds narrower than 1,500 km/s, the corresponding incidence limits are 13% and 19% at 95% confidence, compared with 31% and 49% locally. Broad Balmer lines are centred on the narrow lines, and Balmer absorbers move below 8% of the escape speed. Published super-Eddington fountain, black-hole-star and quasi-star models each fail a measured property of the spectra. LRDs and LBDs drive no superwinds, and their black holes grow without the wind feedback invoked to regulate galaxies.

papers.title: Sharp Transitions of Copy Complexity in Local Certification of Typical Pure States
papers.abstract: We determine the asymptotic copy complexity of $n$-qudit state certification with tensor-product measurements. For given acceptance and rejection fidelities $a$ and $b$ ($b<a$), the optimal copy complexity is $\Theta(n^r)$. For each qudit dimension $d$, $r$ is a piecewise constant function of $g=(a-b)/(1-b)$. This scaling holds for a family of sets of pure target states whose Haar measures tend to one as $n\to\infty$. We characterize the range of $g$ corresponding to each optimal exponent and provide an algorithm for computing its endpoints exactly. The optimal exponent grows logarithmically with $1/g$ as $g$ tends to zero. The upper bound is achieved by a nonadaptive protocol using only single-qudit projective measurements and classical postprocessing. The matching lower bound is established by constructing pairs of states that are difficult to distinguish under arbitrary tensor-product measurements. Our result can thus guide the design of certification tests when the number of available copies is limited.

papers.title: ELMO: Emergent Representations In Imitation Learning Via Dynamic Hierarchical Action Chunking
papers.abstract: Robot trajectories naturally decompose into variable-length phases with distinct semantic intents, such as reaching, grasping, and lifting. However, training policies to minimize MSE treats all actions as equal, obscuring their semantic structure. While latent action models attempt to create a structured prediction target by compressing action chunks into latent representations, existing approaches rely on two-stage training and context-blind decoders. Consequently, their representations are context-agnostic motion codes (e.g., "move down") which fail to capture behavioural intent (e.g., "pick up the block"). To overcome these bottlenecks, we introduce the Emergent Latent-action MOdel (ELMO), an end-to-end framework that encodes robot trajectories as grounded semantic codes -- representations that ground task-level behavioural intent in the current environment. ELMO jointly trains a VLA planner and an observation-conditioned decoder over dynamically chunked trajectories, learning a semantically grounded action space without separate pretraining. Across standard benchmarks, ELMO outperforms comparable prior methods by 9.6 percentage points on LIBERO-Plus and by 0.75 in average task length on CALVIN. Furthermore, on Blocks -- our shortcut-free simulation and real-world generalization benchmark -- ELMO reaches a 38.6% success rate while all baselines remain below 5%, demonstrating its ability to capture the semantic structure of demonstrations. Website: https://uoft-isl.github.io/elmo.github.io/

papers.title: Unitary Synthesis with a Unary Tracker
papers.abstract: This manuscript studies general unitary synthesis using unary-encoded ancillary register. Our first construction focuses on the $T$-cost of unitary synthesis. We maintain a unary register that coherently tracks the computational-basis label of the data. This allows Boolean lookups to use only CNOTs and shares the precision-dependent synthesis cost across the branches of each cosine-sine decomposition (CSD) factor. For a classically specified $n$-qubit unitary with $K$ mixing branches in its CSD, we obtain $T$-count $O(K+NL)$ using $N+O(L)$ clean ancillas, where $N=2^n$ and $L=n+\log(1/\epsilon)$. We also give a related construction that directly applies the unitary onto a unary register to implement disjoint branches in parallel. Combining this with the quantum Shannon decomposition gives space-depth volume $O(N^2)$ using arbitrary single-qubit gates and CNOTs, which matches the asymptotically optimal bound.

papers.title: Was the Model Given the Right Action? Auditing and Repairing Action Interfaces in Navigation World Models
papers.abstract: World models are evaluated by predicting future observations from actions. These evaluations assume that actions are prepared the same way as during training, but an unchecked mismatch can make a model appear less accurate than it is. We audit this assumption in Navigation World Models (NWM) and find three interacting differences between its training and rollout code. Correcting the inputs, without retraining, reduces mean visual prediction error by 42%, measured with DreamSim on the RECON navigation dataset. The correction also changes the ranking of NWM checkpoints in an exploratory analysis and removes or reduces two alternative models' measured advantages. Correcting only the normalization offset instead increases error, showing why interacting mismatches must be checked together. To test whether sensitivity to input preparation extends beyond NWM, we deliberately introduce encoding errors into two alternative models; both become less accurate. We introduce ActRosetta, a tool that checks whether action encoding matches training, identifies supported causes of disagreement, and repairs inputs when sufficient information is available. Repair helps little where predictions barely respond to actions, the tool's diagnosis has limited coverage, and improved control remains unproven. For any action-conditioned world model, the lesson is the same: before reporting rollout error, verify that evaluation encodes actions exactly as training did.

papers.title: Left-Invariant Kundt Structures on Almost Abelian Lie Groups
papers.abstract: We study left-invariant Kundt structures on almost abelian Lie groups. We establish algebraic existence criteria and characterize the admissible real Jordan forms according to the signature of the Abelian ideal. We then characterize the Kundt pairs defining pp-waves and plane waves in arbitrary dimension, with particular attention to recurrent and parallel null directions. Examples in dimension four illustrate both plane and non-plane pp-wave geometries.

papers.title: Recursive Word Conditioning for Higher-Dimensional Partitions: Exact Enumeration and Complexity
papers.abstract: Let $p_d(n)$ denote the number of $d$-dimensional partitions of weight $n$. We develop an exact enumeration method operating on recursively parsed partition words (which are shown to encode $d$-dimensional partitions), beginning with an elementary interior-part decomposition of ordinary partitions. Conditioning on an interior word block separates the preceding and succeeding nested blocks. For higher-dimensional partitions, transversely re-parsing the preceding words permits the same conditioning operation to be iterated. Recursive containment and joins carry effective floors across the cuts, while a nonnegative excess permits exact truncation and pruning. The resulting procedure is a complete row-conditioning algorithm. For every fixed $d\ge3$, we prove that it computes $p_d(0),\ldots,p_d(N)$ using at most $\exp\!\bigl(O_d(N^{(d-1)/(d+1)}\log(N+2))\bigr)$ arithmetic operations. A diagonal refinement replaces the final row-conditioning stages by coupled interlacing chains of ordinary-partition words and sharpens the bound to $\exp\!\bigl(O_d(N^{(d-1)/(d+1)})\bigr)$. The algorithms count constrained completions through reusable weight-indexed coefficients rather than enumerating finished partitions. Exact computations with these algorithms reach weights 100, 50, 45, 40 and 35 in dimensions 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, respectively. On a single 2.1\,GHz core the program computes $p_3(0),\ldots,p_3(100)$ in under four hours and each of the tables in dimensions 4--7 in under 30 minutes.

papers.title: On the Density of Repeated Entries in Pascal's Triangle
papers.abstract: Let $N(a)$ denote the number of occurrences of the integer $a>1$ in Pascal's triangle, and set ${\mathcal E}_H=\{a\geq3:N(a)>2H\}$, $A_H(x)=|{\mathcal E}_H\cap[1,x]|.$ For every fixed $K\geq2$ we prove the expansion $A_1(x)=\sum_{k=2}^{K}(k!x)^{1/k}+O_K\!\left(x^{1/(K+1)}\right).$ Consequently, the Dirichlet series ${D}_1(s)=\sum_{a\in{\mathcal E}_1}a^{-s}$ extends meromorphically to $\Re s>0$, with simple poles precisely at $s=1/k$, $k\geq2$, of residue $(k!)^{1/k}/k$. For every $H\geq2$, $x\ge 3$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, we prove $A_H(x)\le A_2(x)\leq\exp\left(\frac{2\log x}{(\log\log x)^{1/4}}\right)\ll_{\varepsilon} x^{\varepsilon}.$ Hence $D_H(s)=\sum_{a\in{\mathcal E}_H}a^{-s}$ is holomorphic for $\Re s>0$ when $H\geq2$, and $\lambda({\mathcal E}_1)=1/2, \lambda({\mathcal E}_H)=0\quad(H\geq2).$ Here, for a set $S\subseteq {\mathbb N}$, its exponent of convergence is $\lambda(S)=\inf\left\{\sigma>0: \sum_{n\in S}n^{-\sigma}<\infty\right\}.$ We also determine the logarithmic-order counting law for the classical Lind--Singmaster family of coefficients of multiplicity at least six.

papers.title: A multi-patch model for sylvatic hematophagous vector dynamics: the impact of landscape anthropization
papers.abstract: We develop a multi-patch model for sylvatic hematophagous vector--(wild) animal interactions with nonlinear migration terms that depend on landscape anthropization. Every patch is a suitable habitat for both animals and vectors, but anthropization reduces the animal carrying capacity and induces animal and vector displacement. We considered three dispersal types. Under unconstrained global dispersal, displaced individuals can move to any other patch. Under the more realistic random and constrained neighbor dispersal, displaced animals move to a neighboring patch chosen either at random or preferentially among less anthropized ones. We parameterized our model for tsetse flies (Glossina spp.) in the districts of Campo, Ny\'e'\'et\'e, and Ma'an, Ocean division, Cameroon. We characterized the equilibria and their local stability analytically for unconstrained global dispersal, and found numerically that, under both neighbor dispersal regimes, populations progressively expand before settling into a stable equilibrium. Under random neighbor dispersal, the effect of anthropization on migration had a much larger impact on steady state densities than its effect on animal carrying capacity. Under constrained neighbor dispersal, populations spread noticeably more slowly, and numerous patches maintained extremely sparse populations. We further investigated invasion speed under different anthropization scenarios. For random neighbor dispersal, invasion times decreased upon introduction of newly anthropized regions, while for constrained neighbor dispersal, anthropized regions either increased or did not affect invasion times. Approximating invasions by pulled traveling waves, we found that anthropized regions act as ``invasion highways'' or ``invasion barriers'' depending on the dispersal type. We conclude that more empirical data on animal dispersal are needed to understand these dynamics.

papers.title: From NP-Hardness to Exact Tractability Through Sample Abundance
papers.abstract: Additional observations can make exact optimization tractable without changing the objective or feasible set. We establish this phenomenon for noisy parity fitting, a worst-case NP-hard problem, with uniformly sampled rank-one sign tensor entries, independent fair factor signs and independent errors. For fixed interaction order $k\ge3$, $n$ signs per block, logarithmic mean degree and known channel biases, $O(n/(\log n)^{1/(k-2)})$ further readings of the same source suffice with high probability for exact optimization in $O(n\log^2 n)$ worst-case work. The leading coefficient is sharp for weak recovery by depth-$O(\log\log n)$ local estimators with independent reading marks. A common signed-field law determines the gain over the generating source, the number of tied optima and the dimension needed for later reweightings. The geometry of the remaining coordinates determines the sharp radius of local verification for high-scoring assignments with high probability.

papers.title: Min-Plus Products and Dynamic Programming with Few Violations of the Adjacent Monge Inequalities
papers.abstract: Local rewards can introduce negative adjacent mixed differences into a convex transition cost. If a cost array $B$ has $s(B)$ such differences, we express it as a Monge array minus $s(B)$ weighted rectangles and sweep its columns, maintaining the lower envelope of the active rows. For explicit finite $n\times n$ matrices $A,B$ and $L=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil$, we compute $A\otimes B$ and the smallest minimizing index for every entry in $\mathcal{O}(n^2L+ns(B)L^3)$ time and $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ space, giving near-quadratic time for arbitrary $A$ when $s(B)=\mathcal{O}(n)$, including right factors with $\Theta(n^2)$ positive differences. For block costs given by a constant-time Monge oracle and $r$ signed rectangle corrections, the sweep activates each row when its prefix optimum becomes available and computes an optimal contiguous partition in $\mathcal{O}((n+r)L^3)$ time and $\mathcal{O}(n+r)$ working space. The sweep handles convex transitions with interval rules and assigns one rectangle to each internal edge or hyperedge reward in a convex block cost, giving near-linear exact algorithms on sparse inputs for ordered graph modularity, weighted contiguous cluster editing, all-or-nothing HyperLam, and bounded-rank strict hypergraph modularity. Let $c_{\mathrm{APSP}}$ denote the deterministic exponent of all-pairs shortest paths with polynomially bounded integer weights. For fixed $3-c_{\mathrm{APSP}}<\alpha\le1$, any deterministic $\mathcal{O}(n^\beta)$-time min-plus product algorithm for polynomially bounded integer matrices with $s(B)\le n^{1+\alpha}$ satisfies $\beta\ge c_{\mathrm{APSP}}-1+\alpha$. The reduction from general integer min-plus multiplication uses right factors obtained from $(j-k)^2$ by at most $n^{1+\alpha}$ interval discounts, with $\Theta(n^2)$ positive differences and all remaining differences negative.

papers.title: A general-purpose electron density model for molecular chemistry
papers.abstract: Universal machine-learning potentials predict molecular structure and stability at the accuracy of quantum mechanics, for a fraction of the cost. Properties derived instead from knowledge of the electronic structure give profound insights into chemical reactivity, but are not accessible with the same ease or transferability. We train PET-rho-OMol25, a model of the ground-state electron density and spin polarization of molecular systems on four million OMol25 structures in multiple charge and spin states. The model makes predictions for entire proteins in a few seconds on a single GPU, and enables estimation of important diagnostics of molecular structure and reactivity, such as vibrational Stark measurements, halogen $\sigma$-holes, hydrogen-bond basicities and core-level shifts, as well as spin density for redox chemistry and magnetism. PET-rho-OMol25 has an accuracy close to density-functional theory, with its least reliable predictions flagged by its built-in uncertainty estimator, for most properties and classes of compounds. It can be used as a drop-in replacement for electronic-structure calculations of the density, making insightful analyses available for larger and more complex structures.

papers.title: Is Gravitational-Wave Waveform Systematics a Bottleneck for Formation Channel Inferences using Effective-Spin and Mass-Ratio?
papers.abstract: Gravitational-wave measurements of the effective spin $\chi_\text{eff}$ and mass ratio $q$ help distinguish binary black hole formation channels, motivating a search for structure in the $\chi_\text{eff} - q$ plane. However, both these quantities are known to be strongly correlated in GW parameter estimation since both enter the leading-order spin-orbit term together, and thus, the detectors cannot easily tell them apart. In this work, we harness the susceptibility of such measurements to waveform systematics by using injection-recovery studies with NRSur7dq4 as the true signal and SEOBNRv5PHM and IMRPhenomTPHM for parameter inferences. Our study shows that, though there can be some parameter space in the $\chi_\text{eff} - q$ plane, primarily in the unequal-mass regime, there can be some impacts from waveform systematics; overall, at a population level, the waveform systematics for the current detectors at their design sensitivity are not a bottleneck in recovering the underlying true population properties. We find that astrophysical properties such as $\chi_\text{eff} - q$ correlations, which are signatures of different formation channels, are unlikely to be spuriously induced by waveform systematics, and inferences about formation channels based on such correlations are likely robust to waveform systematics at present, though some events that are in the parameter space of large impact can show some outlier behaviour. We find that some of the GW events such as GW190403$\_$051519 and GW240527$\_$230910 are in the vicinity of the $\chi_\text{eff} - q$ parameter space, where large waveform systematics can arise, and these events are more susceptible to waveform systematics than others in GWTC-5. This study will play a vital role in precision astrophysical population inference from GW data in the future and in assessing the possibility of waveform systematics.

papers.title: WorldInteract: Controllable Streaming Video Generation for Multi-Material Interactions
papers.abstract: Video world models aim to create interactive physical worlds that capture how diverse materials move and interact. Yet material-dependent dynamics remain underexplored in controllable video generation, limiting reliable control in scenes with different materials. We present WorldInteract, a streaming video generation framework that decomposes cross-material interaction into material-dependent behavior generation and contact response computation. External pushes and contact impulses are expressed through a shared velocity-increment interface, allowing material behaviors learned from interaction-free videos to be reused in interacting scenes. A physics controller predicts contacts and computes velocity increments from estimated masses and restitution coefficients, while a causal generator executes these increments using learned material behaviors. This separation enables cross-material interaction without supervised contact videos spanning diverse material pairings and contact configurations. We train the generator on 30k simulated interaction-free videos spanning 22 material classes and introduce Material-Aware RL, using verifiable physical rewards to refine material behavior and control execution. WorldInteract substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods on Physics-IQ and delivers more reliable push control on real-world images.

papers.title: Observation of a F\"orster Resonance in a Heated Rydberg Atom Ensemble
papers.abstract: Rydberg atoms in thermal vapour are of increasing relevance for a range of emerging technologies including compact electric field sensors, where state energies are detected via electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT). However, at increased atomic number densities, the Rydberg EIT response becomes non-linear, resulting in distortion of the spectral lineshape. It is thought that this non-linearity mainly arises due to ionisation, although accurate quantitative modelling of the spectrum and assessment of other physical processes remains challenging. In this work, we address these issues in a combined theoretical and experimental study, constructing a model that accurately reproduces observed EIT spectral profiles. We show from analysis of lineshape shifts that while ionisation accounts for most of the non-linearity, it is also possible to observe Rydberg interaction effects for strongly-coupled states near a F\"orster resonance.

papers.title: Low-degree hardness rules out eigenvalue tests but not eigenvector tests
papers.abstract: We study what low-degree hardness implies for spectral tests, with the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE) as the null distribution. We show that, once a fixed amount of Gaussian noise is added, it rules out every test based on eigenvalues, but not tests based on eigenvectors. For eigenvalues, if the low-degree advantage vanishes at logarithmic degree, then the joint law of the noisy eigenvalues converges to that of the GOE in total variation. For eigenvectors, we construct planted distributions with vanishing low-degree advantage whose eigenvalues follow the GOE law exactly at every noise level, yet whose noisy eigenvectors still distinguish them from the GOE. A single eigenvector can suffice. After a small amount of noise, a polynomial-time test that uses only the span of a fixed fraction of the top eigenvectors also succeeds, even when the low-degree advantage vanishes at a prescribed polylogarithmic degree. To prove the eigenvalue result, we split the noise into three increments. The first uses the low-degree assumption to establish eigenvalue rigidity. The second couples the two spectra through Dyson Brownian motion and applies homogenization to obtain a transport estimate. The third uses Gaussian smoothing to convert this estimate into closeness in total variation.

papers.title: Tensor products of finite groups without compatibility conditions are finite
papers.abstract: It has been an open question whether Inassaridze's tensor product $G\otimes H$ is finite whenever $G$ and $H$ are finite. In this paper, we answer this question in the affirmative, and, as a consequence, we prove that the low dimensional nonabelian homology groups $H_i(G,A)$, $i=0,1$, are finite whenever $G$ and $A$ are finite. We achieve this by introducing a much more general tensor product $G\bt H$, defined for groups acting on themselves and on each other by arbitrary automorphisms, with no compatibility conditions, and subject only to the two defining relations of the nonabelian tensor product. We prove that $G\bt H$ is finite whenever $G$ and $H$ are finite. Since the nonabelian tensor product of Brown and Loday, Inassaridze's tensor product and the box-tensor product are all quotients or special cases of $G\bt H$, this brings the finiteness results for all these tensor products under one umbrella.

papers.title: Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks
papers.abstract: The emerging field of weight space learning has demonstrated the potential to enable metanetworks, i.e. models that process neural network (NN) data, to support several steps of the machine learning lifecycle, from model optimisation to evaluation and adaptation. However, this potential has yet to materialise beyond small-scale MLPs or CNNs: most current models, including message-passing based graph metanetworks (GMNs), operate exclusively at the finest level of granularity, processing every neuron and weight of the input model. Their cost therefore scales with the number of parameters. Yet NNs are inherently organised hierarchically, with neurons forming layers and layers forming blocks and modules. Additionally, several of their properties, such as Lipschitz upper bounds and generalisation measures, are compositions of layer- and block-level quantities. To incorporate this inductive bias, we introduce Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks (H-GMNs), which leverage the input architecture's hierarchy to coarsen and refine the graph using permutation-symmetry-preserving pooling and un-pooling layers. Further, we extend H-GMNs to Transformers by introducing a graph construction that preserves permutation symmetries and enables multi-level pooling. Our evaluation includes new ResNet-18, ViT and varying ViT model zoos of up to 86M parameters, on tasks spanning model evaluation (an analytic Lipschitz bound proxy, generalisation and robustness prediction), testing (backdoor detection) and editing (pruning). Experimental results show that, compared to non-equivariant alternatives and flat GMNs, H-GMNs are markedly more sample-efficient, and their cost remains nearly constant as metanetwork depth grows, allowing deeper and more expressive processing where flat GMNs run out of memory, without compromising accuracy, which in certain cases considerably improves.

papers.title: Bigger Model or Bigger Table? How Much Backbone a Chorus N-gram Module Replaces
papers.abstract: We ask how much of a transformer's backbone the Chorus N-gram module replaces. Chorus adds hashed tables of token bigrams and trigrams to its input and attention. We train models of 16M to 349M parameters on 1.34 billion tokens of Polish printed before 1918 and find the size of a plain model with the same held-out loss. A separate learning-rate search for each kind of model cuts Chorus's gain at 47M by about a third. With tables about as large as the backbone, Chorus then matches a plain model 1.34 times its size at 16M and 1.16 to 1.20 times from 107M to 349M. With these tables, each added parameter replaces at most 0.31 backbone parameters. Chorus trains slower than a plain model of its size and faster than one of the same loss. On a fact quiz the two differ about as much as two seeds of one model. The results rest on one corpus, one 8,000-token vocabulary and a fifth of an epoch.

papers.title: LiDAR Intensity Reconstruction with Limited Real Data: An Architecture Benchmark under Fixed-Epoch Training
papers.abstract: Physics-derived simulation can supplement scarce real-world LiDAR intensity measurements, but its effectiveness depends on the learning architecture and the amount of real training data available. We benchmark nine neural architectures for LiDAR intensity reconstruction from depth, semantic labels, incidence angle, and material reflectance, using real SemanticKITTI and synthetic VoxelScape range-image data. All models follow a fixed 20-epoch protocol; this controls the number of training passes, not the computational cost across architectures. We report mean absolute error (MAE), mean squared error (MSE), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity (SSIM), inference timing, and spectral-energy agreement. We also evaluate four selected architectures with fixed-size training mixtures containing 0\%, 1\%, 5\%, 10\%, 20\%, 50\%, or 100\% real frames. With real-only training, UNet-V2 achieves the best reported reconstruction metrics (MAE 0.234, MSE 0.140, PSNR 8.64 dB, and SSIM 0.647), followed by a denoising diffusion model (DDPM). In several mixtures containing 1--10\% real data, DDPM achieves lower error and higher image-quality metrics than the evaluated deterministic alternatives, whereas UNet-V2 leads with 100\% real data. Spectral analysis additionally reveals architecture-dependent discrepancies across frequency bands. These findings characterize reconstruction trade-offs under the stated data mixtures and fixed-epoch protocol, without establishing compute-matched superiority or isolating the diffusion objective from backbone differences.

papers.title: Robust Recourse under Causal Graph Ambiguity
papers.abstract: Causal algorithmic recourse recommends actions to reverse unfavorable decisions by modeling how interventions change an individual's features. Existing methods typically assume one causal graph that describes the system and account for uncertainty in the causal mechanisms. However, there usually exist several graphs that fit the same data but can predict different effects for the same action. Certain actions may achieve recourse across multiple graphs, but as the set of potential graphs grows, a single best action may become infeasible. We propose Worst-Case Recourse and Graph-Weighted Recourse to find a low-cost action that succeeds across all candidate graphs or a specified fraction of graph weight, respectively. Assuming a set of plausible graphs, for each graph we fit Gaussian process structural equations and assess success using the posterior mean--standard-deviation criterion. We use gradient-based search to determine minimal cost actions and check the validity of the actions on fresh posterior samples. In synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks, relaxing robustness, the requirement that an action succeed under every candidate graph, can increase the number of valid recommendations for recourse and lower costs of actions for both methods. In the 20-node GP benchmark, relaxation increases the number of factual instances offered recourse (coverage) from 341 to 436 out of 1,000, while the number of true successes, actions that flip the decision under the generating model, falls from 251 to 184, illustrating the coverage--validity trade-off. Accounting for graph ambiguity can help decision-makers recommend actions that remain effective even when the causal mechanisms of the system are not fully known.

papers.title: How Large are Monetary Policy Effects? dentifying the Shocks in a VAR also Identifies the Constants
papers.abstract: Restrictions on the contemporaneous effects matrix used to identify fundamental shocks in a structural VAR, also determine the mapping from the structural constant terms to the reduced form constant terms. In some models one will have priors about these structural constant terms and these should therefore be included in a Bayesian estimation procedure. We illustrate the potential significance of this using the analysis of monetary policy by Baumeister and Hamilton (2018) as a motivating example. We show that imposing priors over the structural constant terms can lead to a more intuitive estimated monetary policy rule and a much larger estimated role for monetary policy in describing the evolution of the data. The analysis also allows for a clear visual presentation of the structural model, highlighting its multiple contending elements. For example the observed inflation series is estimated to be the result of positive demand and commodity price effects offset by negative monetary policy and risk spread effects.

papers.title: Privileged On-Policy Distillation for Calibrated Alzheimer's Diagnosis With Missing Modalities
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease is diagnosed from clinical, biospecimen and imaging evidence, but few patients undergo every test. Because these modalities are complementary, a missing one has many plausible values. Most existing methods leave it out or train on one estimate, so their classifier never sees its other values, and the estimate is never checked against the diagnosis. We address both gaps with on-policy distillation: the model fills in the missing modalities itself, and teachers with information available only in training grade these fills. Our method, Graded Rollout Imputation with Privileged teachers, draws several fills, one modality at a time. An imputation teacher that knows the diagnosis grades each step, bringing the outcome into the imputation as statistical practice recommends. A diagnosis teacher that sees all real modalities supplies a soft target. Trained on fills that vary, the model learns a confidence that reflects what the missing tests leave open, and it diagnoses from a single rollout. On the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohort, it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. On two external cohorts, it remains competitive in discrimination and, even after every method is recalibrated, its calibration error is level with the lowest on both. Added to three of these baselines, the teachers improve each of them. Our method offers a single, well-calibrated model for whatever combination of tests a patient has received.

papers.title: NASA's Pandora SmallSat Mission: Gaussian Processes for Simulated Stellar Heterogeneity Corrections under Imperfect Stellar Models
papers.abstract: Stellar contamination is the primary bottleneck limiting robust atmospheric characterization of exoplanets orbiting active K- and M-dwarfs with James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) transmission spectroscopy. Launched in January 2026, NASA's Pandora SmallSat mission addresses this challenge through long-term, simultaneous visible photometry and near-infrared spectroscopy of planet-hosting stars, providing the data to disentangle planetary and stellar signals. However, conventional stellar-contamination corrections rely on stellar atmosphere models, making them vulnerable to model inaccuracies that can impede accurate inferences. Here, we investigate how Pandora data can be used to mitigate stellar contamination without an accurate host star model. We present a Gaussian-process-aided stellar retrieval framework that learns wavelength-dependent deviations from current stellar model grids. We propagate stellar contamination factors directly from the stellar retrieval into the planetary atmospheric retrievals, allowing the atmospheric inference to marginalize over stellar-contamination uncertainty without relying on a biased stellar model. Tests using simulated Pandora observations with realistic stellar model mismatch show that this framework consistently improves the recovery of disk-integrated stellar spectra. For a WASP-69 b-like system, this approach can reduce model-driven biases in inferred atmospheric properties, though degeneracies among stellar and atmospheric parameters can leave residual biases. This flexible, data-driven framework is a promising approach toward accurate stellar-contamination corrections and more robust atmospheric inference even when host-star model grids are inaccurate.

papers.title: Reading, Not Adapting: Unlocking Frozen Visual Knowledge for AI-Generated Image Detection
papers.abstract: Generalization to unseen image generators has driven efforts to adapt pretrained visual representations for detection. Yet recent findings show that vision foundation models already encode transferable detection knowledge, while further adaptation can impair generalization. This motivates a shift from backbone adaptation to knowledge readout. Conventional linear probing offers a direct way to read this knowledge but is limited to final-layer RGB features. Multi-cue detectors broaden the evidence base, but their designs introduce other tradeoffs: adaptation may compromise pretrained transferability, heterogeneous encoders complicate feature integration, and late fusion precludes intermediate cross-view interaction. To overcome these limitations, we propose ReMoT, a Mixture-of-Transformers-inspired framework that reads complementary knowledge from spatially aligned RGB and wavelet views within a fully frozen visual foundation. ReMoT employs staged joint attention to enable controlled local and global cross-view interaction, while learnable fusion queries progressively read complementary evidence across Transformer depth without writeback. ReMoT achieves 91.2% average accuracy across eight benchmark groups with 3,074 trainable parameters, attaining the highest overall average among the evaluated methods. These results support structured knowledge readout as a promising alternative to backbone adaptation. Code is available at https://github.com/yunncheng/ReMoT.

papers.title: ENSO-linked redistribution of post-monsoon tropical cyclone energy between the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal: 1982--2025
papers.abstract: Tropical cyclones in the North Indian Ocean (NIO) form in two sub-basins, the Arabian Sea (AS) and the Bay of Bengal (BoB), which are usually studied separately, with their relationship to the El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) treated as stationary. We develop a joint inter-basin statistical framework and apply it to 416 disturbances from quality-controlled IBTrACS best tracks for 1982--2025, with harmonised IMD and JTWC intensities, ERA5 and ERSSTv5. The framework tests whether ENSO changes the basin total or redistributes energy between the sub-basins, separates its effect on formation from that on intensification, attributes each sub-basin's response to environmental terms along individual tracks, and tests stationarity and the record length needed to detect trends. In October-December, ENSO redistributes rather than changes the total: for a one-standard-deviation increase in Ni\~no-3.4 (about 1 $^\circ$C), accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) is multiplied by 1.89 in the AS and by 0.63 in the BoB, while the NIO total shows no detectable change (factor 0.99 [0.74, 1.32]). ENSO acts on intensification, with no detectable effect on formation: the odds that a cyclonic storm becomes very severe rise about fourfold in the AS and halve in the BoB, through lower vertical wind shear (VWS) over the AS and weaker low-level vorticity over the BoB. The relationship has changed: El Ni\~no lowered total NIO energy in 1982--2003, but in 2004-2025 AS gains balanced BoB losses (change p = 0.016). Very severe storms and rapid intensification increased in the AS only, and no 15-year window detects this increase, so about three decades of data are needed. The post-monsoon IOD signal can hardly be separated from ENSO, and August Ni\~no-3.4 gives modest skill for the AS-BoB partition but none for the basin total.

papers.title: A 2D fluid model in BOUT++/Hermes-3 for simulating detached divertor plasmas in tokamaks
papers.abstract: Detached divertor operation is essential for controlling target heat fluxes in future high-power tokamaks. We present a two-dimensional fluid model implemented in BOUT++/Hermes-3 for simulating detached divertor plasmas with plasma-neutral interactions and fixed-fraction impurity radiation. We report improvements to the PETSc SNES-based steady-state solver used for two-dimensional axisymmetric transport simulations with fluid neutrals and assess the performance of several sparse-solver preconditioning strategies. For the cases considered here, STRUMPACK used as an ILU preconditioner with low-rank compression provides the most favorable performance, reducing the linear-to-nonlinear iteration ratio and achieving approximately a fivefold speedup relative to \HYPRE{}-based configurations. The optimized solver is then applied to DIII-D shot $\#174287$ at 4000~ms to characterize detached divertor conditions. Cross-field transport coefficients are adjusted to reproduce upstream experimental profiles, and detachment is modeled using nitrogen fixed-fraction radiation. Steady-state particle and energy balances are evaluated by decomposing the density and pressure equations into their transport and source terms. In the outer divertor, electron energy losses are dominated by ionization and impurity radiation, while ion energy losses occur mainly through collisional transfer to electrons. An upstream separatrix density scan shows decreasing target electron temperature and a rollover of the integrated target ion saturation current at higher $n_{e,\mathrm{sep}}$ consistent with expected detachment trends. These developments establish a foundation for future multispecies simulations. Hermes-3 is publicly available on GitHub under the GPL-3 open-source license.

papers.title: Characterisations of symmetric Birkhoff--James orthogonality via numerical ranges
papers.abstract: Birkhoff-James orthogonality in a normed space is in general not symmetric. For a complex Banach space $\mathscr{X}$ of dimension at least $2$, we prove that the following assertions are equivalent: Birkhoff-James orthogonality in $\mathscr{X}$ is symmetric; the spatial numerical range of every operator on $\mathscr{X}$ coincides with its reverse numerical range, defined by reversing the orthogonality; $\mathscr{X}$ has the simultaneous zero inclusion property, that is, $0$ lies in the closure of the numerical range of an invertible operator exactly when it lies in that of its inverse; $\mathcal{B}(\mathscr{X})$ has the analogous property for the algebra numerical range; and a simple inequality for supporting functionals holds. This confirms a conjecture of Ghosh. We also introduce the asymmetry constant $R(\mathscr{X})\in[1,2]$, as the supremum of the norms of the projections $I-x\otimes\xi$, where $x$ is a unit vector and $\xi$ is a supporting functional at $x$. We show that $R(\mathscr{X})^{-1}$ is the radius of the largest ball around the identity on which the simultaneous zero inclusion property holds, and that every number in $[1,2]$ is the asymmetry constant of some two-dimensional $\ell^p$ space.

papers.title: R\'enyi multi-entropy from Riemann surfaces
papers.abstract: We compute vacuum tripartite R\'enyi multi-entropy in a two-dimensional compact-boson conformal field theory (CFT). For every integer R\'enyi index $n\geq2$, we evaluate the partition function on the replica Riemann surface for disjoint intervals, obtaining the twist four-point function in terms of a ratio of theta functions. An independent calculation of the partition function on a Fermat curve yields the adjacent three-point coefficient. In the fusion limit, the Riemann surface for disjoint intervals degenerates into two Fermat curves, and the residue of the four-point function reproduces the squared three-point coefficient, as required by the operator product expansion. The genuine multi-entropy therefore approaches twice its strictly adjacent value. The CFT predictions agree with lattice calculations for the critical XXZ and Ising spin chains and a harmonic chain. We also exhibit a unitary CFT in which the canonical replica construction yields complex R\'enyi multi-entropy.

papers.title: Higher-Order Generation of First-Order Theories
papers.abstract: We introduce a logic whose formulae are finite descriptions of possibly infinite first-order theories. A theory is a set of first-order sentences, generated in our setting by a higher-order recursion scheme. Such a scheme is a finite grammar whose parameters may denote trees or operations on trees. We consider two interpretations: a model must satisfy every generated sentence under the conjunctive interpretation, and at least one under the disjunctive interpretation. For schemes of order $k=0$, these theories coincide with the regular first-order theories of Mathur et al. (POPL 2025). We generalize this representation by allowing higher-order schemes, while retaining first-order quantification in every generated sentence. We study the expressive power, model checking, and satisfiability of this logic. Over finite ordered structures, we show that disjunctive theories of existential sentences generated at order at most $k$ capture $k$-EXPTIME, for every $k\geq0$. Allowing unrestricted first-order sentences captures $(k+1)$-EXPTIME at the same scheme order, where $0$-EXPTIME denotes polynomial time. We also give model-checking algorithms in the corresponding time classes for each fixed signature, variable-name set, and order bound. For satisfiability under either interpretation, we extend several decidability results for regular theories to every order. However, we show that conjunctive satisfiability of quantifier-free theories, decidable at order zero, becomes undecidable already at order one. Finally, we recover decidable conjunctive satisfiability at every order by separating higher-order generation of Boolean structure from independent regular generation of ground atoms. Together, these results show how higher-order generation of first-order syntax captures the exponential-time hierarchy while retaining decidable satisfiability in restricted fragments.

papers.title: From Spin Glass Theory to Optimization in High Dimensions and Modern Artificial Neural Networks
papers.abstract: This chapter pays tribute to Giorgio Parisi by reviewing the influence of his work on spin glasses and replica symmetry breaking (RSB) on combinatorial optimization and artificial neural networks. We first introduce replica and cavity methods through the matching and traveling salesman problems, before discussing random satisfiability and the development of survey propagation. We then examine applications to neural networks, emphasizing the connections between the geometry of solution spaces, computational hardness, and learning. Particular attention is given to rare regions of high local entropy and their role in algorithmic accessibility. Examples involving overparameterized models and asymmetric recurrent networks illustrate how these ideas connect constrained optimization and inference with concepts developed in spin-glass theory.

papers.title: Gaussian Processes for Optimal Space-Filling Input Design
papers.abstract: The quality of a model resulting from (black-box) system identification is highly dependent on the quality of the data that is used during the identification procedure. As nonlinear system identification is sensitive to modeling and extrapolation errors, having experiments that explore the considered operation range of interest are of high importance. The Gaussian-Process based space-filling input design strategy introduces an experiment design technique that aims to achieve a space-filling distribution within the argument space of a (nonlinear) approximator used for modeling the true system. Experiments carried out on simulation examples show that models trained with space-filling signals generalize better over the region of interest compared to models obtained from non-space-filling experiments. Moreover, the method is connected to the optimality theory of experiment design (V- and D-optimal design), allowing the experimenter to tailor the designed space-filling signal to maximize its information content with respect to the experiment objective.

papers.title: Spec2Weights: Certifying Networks that a Language Model Writes from a Specification
papers.abstract: A language model can write the weights of a small MLP, CNN, RNN or GNN from a plain-language specification, with no data and no gradient step. We ask when such a network can be proved exact in the float32 arithmetic it actually runs in.
