We measure the limits of duration perception from audio against a human baseline to address this gap. Drawing from psychophysics, we operationalise duration perception as a melody recognition task, testing when a melody becomes unrecognisable as it is slowed down. Of 21 tested models, most cannot recognise well-known melodies without labelled in-context examples. With in-context examples, seven recognise melodies reliably, most peaking within the median human recognition band. Generalisation is limited: (i) recognition peaks shift with in-context example speed, (ii) melody titles induce prediction bias, and (iii) providing examples with scientific pitch notation does not prevent accuracy declining at long note durations for most models. In humans, the recognition window is a property of the perceiver; in current models, it is largely a property of the prompt.

papers.title: Feature-Based Explainability of Transformer Scoring Models: A Fidelity-First Framework for Automated Writing Assessment
papers.abstract: Transformer-based automated writing scoring models can achieve strong agreement with human scores while providing limited transparency into the response characteristics associated with their predictions. This study evaluated a feature-based post-hoc explanation approach in which explanatory fidelity was established before feature importance was interpreted. English Language Arts responses from three writing prompts in Grades 6 and 8 were analyzed, with about 12,700 responses per prompt and separate DeBERTa-v3-base research models for Expression and Conventions. Each response was represented by 61 interpretable linguistic and writing-quality features. Four approaches - theory-driven composites, hierarchical feature groupings, exploratory factor analysis, and Random Forest surrogates - were compared in their ability to reproduce DeBERTa predictions. Random Forest surrogates produced the largest observed R2 values across all six prompt-by-trait conditions, with held-out R2 values from .81 to .95. SHAP analyses showed substantial overlap in high-importance features across traits, with 75% to 90% of the top 20 features shared. Trait differentiation occurred mainly through relative feature weighting: Expression showed greater importance for lexical and conceptual indicators, whereas Conventions showed greater importance for sentence-level and syntactic-control indicators. Under researcher-defined mappings, rubric correspondence was 90%-95% for Expression and 12%-18% for Conventions. These percentages are descriptive and conditional on the mappings and available linguistic features. The findings support a fidelity-first framework for examining apparent scoring priorities while distinguishing post-hoc evidence about model behavior from direct explanation of transformer internals.

papers.title: MGMem: An Efficient, Deterministic, and Provenance-Preserving Framework for Long-Horizon Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Long-horizon Large Language Model (LLM) agents need persistent memory that surfaces the right past interaction at the right time across thousands of turns. Many systems index by invoking generative LLMs to rewrite history into summaries, facts, or knowledge graphs--a step that is (a) costly (thousands of generative calls per build), (b) non-deterministic (undermining reproducibility and giving inconsistent answers across runs), and (c) provenance-erasing (the reader sees synthesized text, not the original turn). We propose MGMem, a framework with no generative indexing calls that replaces this step with a deterministic discriminative-parser pipeline: recurring mentions across sessions are organized into an incidence graph, question mentions are resolved by a subject-conditioned three-stage resolver, and raw dialogue episodes are returned to the reader. On English multi-session dialogue QA, MGMem outperforms matched-protocol baselines on LoCoMo without generative indexing calls; on the full LongMemEval-S, it remains competitive overall and leads or ties on single-session types among local retrieval comparisons. Code: https://github.com/junhong-h/MGMem

papers.title: The Bundesrat corpus: A dataset of political discourse in the German Federal Council
papers.abstract: The Bundesrat is Germany's second legislative chamber and a constitutional veto player within its political system. The members of the Bundesrat are delegates of state governments. Tracing the political discourse in the Bundesrat is challenging as it has a limited machine-readable corpus available. To address this issue, we present a speaker-attributed corpus of 1,067 Bundesrat plenary sessions from the chamber's first session on 7 September 1949 to 10 July 2026. In this period, a total of 53,362 speeches by 2,473 individuals were delivered in the chamber, including written statements. Each speech includes a speech ID, the full German text, the speaker's name, the date and location of the session, the federal state that the speaker represents, the speaker's role (if applicable), the type of contribution, and the speaker's gender. The dataset provides interdisciplinary research opportunities across computational political science, legislative studies, and parliamentary discourse analysis, coupled with discourse from the Bundestag.

papers.title: On the Tragedy of the Commons in Heterogeneous Distributed Resource Allocation
papers.abstract: We consider the Tragedy of the Commons (ToC) problem, which commonly arises in heterogeneous distributed resource allocation, in which selfish users are independently interested in optimizing their own utility. Such self-interested decision-making in decentralized settings often results in inefficient resource utilization because users prefer high-capacity resources, leading to their overutilization. We cast the problem into a non-cooperative game and derive closed-form characterizations of both the distributed Nash equilibrium (NE) and the socially optimal allocation. In view of these closed-form expressions, we establish the structural conditions under which the ToC arises, and derive an exact expression for the Price of Anarchy (PoA). We further prove that the PoA can become arbitrarily large (unbounded) under suitable traffic conditions. Motivated by these observations, we propose a penalty-based incentive mechanism that discourages the use of overloaded servers while preserving decentralized decision-making. We analyze the resulting equilibrium load redistribution and establish conditions under which the proposed mechanism reduces the overall system cost and improves equilibrium efficiency.

papers.title: Bohr inequalities and Landau-type estimates for harmonic Poisson extensions of $L^p$ boundary functions
papers.abstract: This paper establishes sharp quantitative bounds governing the Bohr phenomenon, Landau-type distortion, and geometric univalence for complex-valued harmonic mappings on the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$ parameterized by boundary data in the Lebesgue spaces $L^{p}(\mathbb{T})$ for $1 \le p \le \infty$, where $\mathbb{T} = \partial\mathbb{D}$. First, we resolve the classical coefficient problem for bounded harmonic mappings by incorporating an integral Parseval constraint rather than crude individual bounds, establishing the sharp Bohr radius as $r_H(a) = \sqrt{(1-a)/(3+a)}$ for a fixed initial term $\vert{}a_0\vert{} = aM$. Second, this framework is extended to the $L^p$ setting under the vanishing normalization $f(0)=0$, explicitly characterizing the sharp Bohr radius as $r_{p} = (2C_{q}+1)^{-1}$, where the structural constant $C_{q}$ is intrinsically linked to the conjugate exponent $q$. Finally, under standard normalization, we determine explicit formulations for both the radius of univalence $r_{0}$ and the corresponding radius of the inscribed Schlicht disk $R_{0}$. The sharpness of all analytical constants and radii is verified through the construction of concrete extremal configurations derived from the Poisson kernel.

papers.title: Halley's Comet Over New Zealand In 1910: An Overview Of A Spectacular Apparition
papers.abstract: Halley's Comet (1P/Halley) returns to the inner Solar System approximately every 76 years. In 1910, the comet put on a particularly wonderful display, whereby the comet attained an apparent magnitude of 1 or brighter, and had a tail of up to 120{\deg} in length. Many New Zealanders saw Comet 1P/Halley and submitted articles to newspapers across the land. Those articles were mostly from lay-people who reported their observations of this, the most famous of all comets. There were, however, numerous serious amateur and professional astronomers who made detailed observations and took world-class photographs of the comet. In this paper, we present the results of a thorough search through historical records and media publications in Aotearoa/New Zealand, to investigate how extensively Comet 1P/Halley was observed from this island nation. Where appropriate, we compare the observations described with international accounts, and find that those made from Aotearoa/New Zealand often echo what observers were witnessing around the world. We find that thousands of New Zealanders observed Comet 1P/Halley in 1910, and that the comet raised the interest in astronomy across the land resulting in the establishment of a number of astronomical societies that remain active to the current day.

papers.title: The Symmetry Budget: How Much Group Structure Should a Network Architecture Assume?
papers.abstract: A network architecture is, in large part, a symmetry assumption: convolution ties weights across translations, attention ties them across permutations, and a fully connected layer ties nothing. When the data are only approximately symmetric, tying trades approximation error against estimation error, and the right amount of tying is a property of the dataset, not of the architecture alone. We study this trade-off in an exactly solvable model: linear maps on signals over the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_d$, with architectures indexed by the subgroup lattice of $\mathbb{Z}_d$, so that a single integer $k \mid d$ interpolates between an unconstrained layer ($k=1$, $d^2$ parameters) and a fully equivariant one ($k=d$, $d$ parameters). We derive the finite-sample excess risk in closed form, show that for a generic symmetry defect the leading-order risk is affine in $1/k$, and prove that intermediate architectures are then never strictly optimal: the lattice collapses to an all-or-nothing choice with phase boundary $n^\star = \sigma^2 d(d-1)/\varepsilon^2$. Structured defects break this collapse and restore interior optima, and we give a closed-form defect profile for a graded defect. Measurements agree with the theory on $60/60$ cells of a $(\varepsilon,n)$ phase diagram and $48/48$ cells of a second phase diagram at $d=16$, recover the predicted exponent as $-1.92$ against $-2$, and exhibit the predicted $k^\star: 12 \to 4 \to 1$ ladder under graded defects; a two-layer nonlinear control reproduces the crossover. We also characterize when the affine collapse survives for non-abelian groups.

papers.title: Temporal Exposure to Byzantine Vulnerability Under Intermittent Participation in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the effect of participation variability on per-round Byzantine vulnerability. We formalise Dynamic Participation Exposure (DPE), a phenomenon in which the global Byzantine fraction remains below an aggregation rule's tolerance threshold, while a participating client set violates, or approaches violation of, the assumptions required for robust aggregation. Under stochastic participation, we derive the probability of per round exposure and analyse how active-set size affects the variability of the observed Byzantine fraction. We further examine the accumulation of exposure over multiple rounds and consider adversaries that selectively participate during favourable rounds. Our analysis shows that intermittent participation does not automatically imply aggregation failure. Rather, it transforms Byzantine robustness from a static population-level property into a stochastic and temporal property. To mitigate this risk, we outline actionable design recommendations based on minimum active-set constraints, temporal monitoring, participation history, and adaptive aggregation.

papers.title: Code availability is not enough: schemas for documenting and extending data analysis
papers.abstract: A data analysis involves a sequence of decisions, from data cleaning to model specification, each of which can affect the reported result. Reproducing that result is not the same as understanding the sequence of decisions that produced it and the reasons for each: the code mixes those decisions with implementation details, while the manuscript states the major decisions and their rationale but scatters them across its sections and often leaves out the minor ones. A reader may then ask how the result would change under a different decision: the question itself is easy to pose, but implementing it is often non-trivial in practice. In this work, we propose a schema that represents a data analysis as a collection of decisions in natural language, from which large language models (LLMs) can generate and validate analysis scripts directly. This workflow can also expand a single analysis into a full multiverse of alternatives, specified in an alternative file, ready for comparison. We demonstrate the proposed workflow in two applications. In the first, we construct a schema for a published regression analysis of heaped smoking data and show that it reproduces the reported estimates, and that a reviewer-suggested alternative can be specified through the alternative file and turned into code automatically. In the second, where no schema is provided, we show how the workflow serves instead as a reproducibility check, applied to the many-analysts football study. As an intermediate representation between the manuscript and code scripts, our schema gives a self-contained account of an analysis and makes it extensible from a reader's perspective.

papers.title: Karhunen-Lo\`{e}ve Expansion of Time-Rescaled Brownian Bridge and Inference of Unit Distribution
papers.abstract: We study the Karhunen-Lo\`{e}ve (KL) basis of the time-rescaled Brownian bridge (TRBB) with time rescales of the form $t\mapsto\int_0^t f^2(s)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s$. For testing unit distributions, we construct a new statistic based on the projection of empirical process onto the KL basis functions of the TRBB and derive its asymptotic distribution. Moreover, using this statistic, we develop a goodness-of-fit test for uniformity and study its power against a specific non-uniform alternative. Numerical experiments indicate that, in the settings considered, the proposed test can have higher power than classical alternatives such as the Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cram\'{e}r-von Mises tests. Furthermore, we propose a two-parameter family of TRBBs and derive the closed-form KL expansion for this new deterministically time-changed process. The family includes a diverse class of monotone rate time rescales, both increasing and decreasing, while retaining a tractable eigenstructure. Finally, an analysis with real data reveals greater flexibility of the proposed parametric family for modelling monotone densities on $[0,1]$.

papers.title: AutoformBench: A Lean Formalization Benchmark for Advanced Mathematics
papers.abstract: AI systems are increasingly capable of producing machine-checked Lean proofs of advanced mathematical results. Real mathematical formalization, however, is not isolated theorem proving: it requires building the definitions and intermediate lemmas that connect a result to a formal library. Existing evaluations often provide isolated theorem statements in settings where much of this supporting theory is already available in Mathlib. We introduce AutoformBench, a benchmark of 341 Lean 4 formalization tasks drawn from 24 advanced mathematical sources. Lean-experienced mathematicians formalized and audited each target statement, leaving the corresponding Lean proof to the evaluated agent. Each problem is embedded in a broader mathematical development: agents receive the informal proof but must translate it into Lean while constructing the missing definitions, intermediate lemmas, and supporting infrastructure. We compare the performance of frontier models on these problems. We find a largely shared difficulty frontier: success depends less on mathematical domain than on models' ability to construct missing formal infrastructure. Data and code at https://github.com/facebookresearch/autoformbench

papers.title: Collective-Influence-Guided Feedback-Vertex-Set Selection for Network Dismantling
papers.abstract: Network dismantling asks for the smallest node set whose removal leaves no connected component larger than a chosen threshold. It is NP-hard, and the heuristics used in practice report margins over one another of a percentage point or two, small enough that attributing a result to the rule that produced it becomes the difficulty. We build a two-phase structural pipeline and use it to make that attribution measurable. Phase~1 decycles the 2-core by depth-first-search back-edge detection, removing one vertex of each certified cycle by its radius-one Collective Influence; Phase~2 fragments the resulting forest by greedy Collective Influence removal. Phase~1 returns a valid feedback vertex set in O(|F|(n+m)) time, and no approximation bound is claimed for the pipeline. Against Random removal, CoreHD, Collective Influence and WEAK-NEIGHBOR on Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi and configuration-model graphs and two real contact networks, the pipeline is competitive with the established heuristics but does not beat them: its best variant is level with WEAK-NEIGHBOR at 0.191 on Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi graphs and ahead of CoreHD's 0.193, a margin of 0.2 points well inside instance-to-instance spread, and it places first on none of the four networks.

papers.title: Quantum Machine Learning for Signature Forgery Detection
papers.abstract: Offline handwritten signatures remain a primary behavioural biometric in legal and financial documents. Detecting skilled forgeries from a static raster image is hard because pen pressure, timing and stroke order are missing. This work studies a family of quantum machine learning pipelines for offline signature forgery detection on a public Kaggle corpus of images split into two classes. We pair a ZZ feature map quantum kernel with three classical learners: K-Nearest Neighbours, Support Vector Machine and Random Forest. We then propose a deeper hybrid that uses EfficientNetB0 as a frozen feature extractor, reduces the resulting 1280 dimensional representation to a qubit register sized subspace through a quantum compatible principal component projection and decides class membership with a nearest neighbour rule. On a single held out test fold the proposed hybrid reaches 92.62 percent accuracy. On stratified five fold cross validation the same pipeline yields a mean accuracy of 91.26 percent with a standard deviation of 1.13 percent. The pipeline keeps a quantum embedding step that is portable to NISQ hardware. We report a controlled ablation across six quantum variants, confusion matrices, a t SNE projection and per class precision, recall and F1 score.

papers.title: Attributing Agentic Failure in Reasoning Vision-Language Models with Interactive 2D Environments
papers.abstract: Agentic benchmarks report a success rate that confounds distinct causes of failure: misreading the environment, never working out how components of the environment operates, operating the components in the wrong order, and failing to recover from a mistake, each of which calls for a different fix. We present an early preview of MultiNet v2.0-Gridworld - an interactive maze environment built for attribution rather than ranking. Four different types of mechanisms, namely key-door pairs, switch-gate pairs, distractors and decoys, and ordered combinations of these mechanisms, can be added, modified, or removed independently while the renderer, the action space, and the scoring function stay fixed. A breadth-first search over the joint state of position, facing direction, inventory, and mechanism state gives every instance an exact optimal action count, which sets its difficulty and grades unfinished episodes. We fix the evaluation protocol on 15 held-out mazes over 540 episodes, then evaluate three vision-language models on 50 mazes. They solve 6 of 150 episodes, 45 of the 50 mazes were not solved by any model, and no episode containing a switch-gate mechanism was solved.

papers.title: Constraint-Aware Test-Time Scoring for LLM and VLM Candidate Selection
papers.abstract: When an LLM or VLM produces several candidate answers, picking the best one usually relies on the model's own confidence, a learned judge model, or a domain check. Each has a known weakness: an answer can be fluent but insecure, mathematically plausible but physically infeasible, or rated highly by a judge while quietly breaking a task requirement. We propose a scoring framework that combines a small set of hard checks every answer must pass with a wider set of softer checks whose scores are blended into one number per candidate. This adaptive scoring framework consists of three components: a drafting model that produces the candidates, a configuring model that selects and weights the checks for each task, and scoring models that rate properties no grounded tool can compute. We apply our proposed method to four tasks: writing code that is both correct and secure (CWEval), generating robot manipulation plans (LIBERO with added safety variants), passing competitive-programming hidden tests (LiveCodeBench), and answering questions from retrieved documents (HotpotQA). An ablation study isolates the contribution of each component and finds that the largest gains come from combining hard checks with candidate comparison: on tasks where the first sampled answer is often broken or unsafe, this pairing lifts joint correctness-and-safety by up to +0.21 (retrieval-augmented QA) and code-generation safety by up to +0.28 (CWEval), with the size of the gain tracking how weak the first sample is, falling to near zero or slightly negative where it is already strong. The per-task layer that selects and weights the softer checks adds no measurable value over simpler alternatives. This builds a unified scoring framework, together with an ablation that identifies the grounded hard checks, not the soft-factor configuration, as the source of the gain.

papers.title: Context Scaling: A New Frontier of AI Scaling
papers.abstract: Many failures of deployed AI arise not from weak inference but from a mismatch between the state a task depends on and the context available when the system acts. Relevant user state, repository revisions, tool traces, sensor readings, or environment changes may be unavailable, distorted, or poorly selected. We call the effort to reduce this bottleneck context scaling. We frame a model as $P_\theta(d\mid c)$ within a system governed by three budgets: training $B_\theta$, decision-time $B_d$, and context-infrastructure $B_c$. Pretraining scaling invests in $\theta$; decision-time scaling searches, refines, or verifies decisions under supplied context; context scaling improves the system's capacity to acquire, represent, deliver, evaluate, and persist deployment state for model use. The three programs interact, but only $B_c$ targets what the system can make available before a decision. This view makes the model-infrastructure pair the unit of analysis. We define effective-context value as a task- and intervention-dependent attribution, separate deployment state from model-visible context, and identify availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization failures. We then organize current mechanisms through a five-operation context lifecycle and propose controlled budget interventions and utility-cost curves for evaluation. The resulting agenda centers on grounded reporting, interaction-data and full-cost infrastructure, and safety and governance for persistent, adaptive systems.

papers.title: Conditional Work Bounds and Timing Evidence for an Industrial NDT Scan Matcher: Cross-Language Work-Trace Conformance
papers.abstract: Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) scan matching has strongly input-dependent execution time on the localization critical path. We study the align kernel of Autoware's production matcher; map loading, preprocessing, and Robot Operating System scheduling are outside the timed scope. Our three-layer method enforces and property-tests a conditional structural work envelope, constructs stress witnesses with deterministic Rust counters, and measures frozen witnesses. It separates algorithmic work from platform time and does not claim a certified hard time bound. A domain-informed construction attains the configured ceiling for the language-common kernel-evaluation term; two archived candidates exercise higher Rust-specific kd-tree traversal at lower common work. Per-input traces define work-trace conformance over passes, processed points, neighbor counts, and leaf identities. Leaf payloads, implementation-specific traversal, total work, and latency remain outside that relation, so C++ results are observations over transferred fixtures rather than a C++ worst-case search. An auxiliary cropped-map, degraded-prior replay exposes the remaining conformance boundary, and a closed-loop replay with recovery shows both engines re-initializing at the same route sections with disjoint coverage bands. In a unified three-boot synthetic campaign, the largest observed values are 988.2 ms for C++ and 610.5 ms for Rust; Rust has the smaller maximum on all 10 paired fixtures. On neighbor-returning fixtures, C++ performs approximately 11 heap allocations per point per derivative pass, whereas the Rust align path allocates none within its reserved envelope. Rust narrows the safe-core verification surface but is not required for bounded execution; its unsafe code, foreign-function interface, and dependencies remain trusted.

papers.title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
papers.abstract: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. Project: https://omniact.github.io/

papers.title: Winning and losing NoGo is PSPACE-complete
papers.abstract: We resolve an open problem of Burke and Hearn and show that the combinatorial game NoGo is PSPACE-complete on grids. This is the usual geometry the game is played on, including at the tournament at a 2011 Banff workshop. In addition to this result, we show that it is also PSPACE-complete under mis\`ere play on grids. We prove both of these results using reductions from Bounded Two-Player Constraint Logic. Finally, we show that it is PSPACE-complete under normal play on connected bipartite subcubic graphs.

papers.title: Anomalies and the Berry Phase: From $\pi^0\to\gamma\gamma$ to the geometry of the fermion vacuum
papers.abstract: We review the chiral anomaly from a historical perspective, from the $\pi^0\to\gamma\gamma$ puzzle and the work of Adler, Bell and Jackiw, to the Wess-Zumino-Witten (WZW) term. We then describe how the WZW term was motivated from quantum chromodynamics in 1983-85. Integrating out the non-Abelian gauge fields, that have a gapped spectrum, gives a Nambu-Jona-Lasinio type theory of quarks, and integrating out the quarks, which are gapped by chiral symmetry breaking, gives the WZW model. The fermion determinant splits into a regulator-dependent modulus, which gives the dynamics of mesons, and a universal phase, which is fixed by the anomaly and is the WZW term. Restricted to the collective coordinates of the baryon soliton, the WZW term imposes a U(1) constraint that makes the baryon wave functions monopole harmonics and fixes their spin, statistics and flavour multiplets. We then explain that this phase is a Berry phase: the Schwinger terms of current algebra are the curvature of a U(1) connection on the space of chiral field configurations, and the WZW term is its holonomy, which we call a Berry-Wilson loop. In 1+1 dimensions we write the connection explicitly in terms of Euler angles, exhibiting a Dirac monopole whose quantised charge is the level of the current algebra.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Can Be Recovered From Its Own Rollouts
papers.abstract: Broadly speaking, reinforcement learning (RL) post-training converts compute into model capabilities by training on model-generated data. Typically, the rollouts are discarded after each update, and the knowledge acquired during RL resides in the model weights. In this work, we investigate how much of this knowledge is retained in the rollouts themselves. A natural first attempt is to replay the original RL algorithm on archived (rather than freshly generated) rollouts, but this generally leads to catastrophic collapse. We provide a simple explanation for this phenomenon, which in turn suggests a remedy we call maximum likelihood replay: fitting the model to its archived rollouts. Surprisingly, starting from the same base model and replaying the rollouts in the order in which they were generated, without any distinction between correct and incorrect responses, is sufficient to recover the performance of online RL. In fact, a single maximum likelihood update per rollout batch closely tracks the entire learning curve of online RL. Furthermore, maximum likelihood replay on the rollouts of the last few RL steps often suffices to recover the final model's performance. This suggests that much of the compute invested in RL goes into discovering an improved sampling distribution rather than learning it from samples.

papers.title: Shifter Quantization: Compact Representations for Native Integer Computation
papers.abstract: Groupwise quantization is used in LLM quantization to improve accuracy at low bit widths, but grouping weights keeps standard integer MMA from spanning the full dot product for efficient GPU inference. We develop a new quantization method, Shifter Quantization (SQ), that reconstructs native-width integer operands by appending and shifting shared bits. To further extend the efficiency, we develop a special variant of SQ, Shifter Integer (SHI), to use INT4 kernels. We show that SQ and SHI formats perform better than standard groupwise quantization in quality, as measured by projection error and KL divergence, and in inference speed, as measured during decoding and prefill. For low precision like 2-bit quantization, SQ2 and SHI2 achieve 2.71-3.77x the 4,096-token prefill throughput of llama.cpp on a Q2_K checkpoint and reduce WikiText-2 KL by 6.6-7.8%. For mid precision like 4-bit quantization, SQ4 achieves 1.43-2.47x the prefill throughput of NInfer's groupwise-integer baselines across the tested models and prompt lengths, with 24-40% lower KL than the NInfer baselines. For high precision like 8-bit quantization, SQ8 achieves 27.4% higher batch-one prefill throughput and 72.7% lower KL than vLLM's online FP8.

papers.title: RFW-W: Scaling Physical Asset Universes for Generative Embodied Simulation
papers.abstract: Scaling embodied simulation requires diverse objects with executable physical representations. We present RFW-W, a physical asset universe connecting rigid, articulated, and deformable asset sources to task-conditioned scene composition. Its reported inventories comprise 1,010,386 asset records: 524,611 rigid assets in 1,212 categories (RFW-R), 402,410 articulated assets in 531 categories (RFW-A), and 83,365 jointly verified deformables in 485 categories (RFW-S). These taxonomies contribute 2,228 dataset--category entries. RFW-R couples category-guided generation with collision geometry, composed physical properties, and interaction annotations; RFW-A uses reusable agent-authored procedural generators with explicit part and joint structure; RFW-S uses structure-aware simulation representations, calibration, and independent testing. A common interface preserves physical requirements specific to each asset type for retrieval and scene assembly. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that RFW-R provides broader asset coverage and stronger scene-fulfillment capabilities than existing datasets. Across five RoboTwin tasks, using 100 demonstrations per task for each asset source, policies trained on RFW-R achieve macro success rates of 71.2% in clean settings and 41.8% under randomization, exceeding the strongest baseline by 15.8 and 10.6 percentage points, respectively. RFW-W provides a scalable and unified asset foundation for generating physically grounded, task-conditioned embodied worlds.

papers.title: LEGOSpec: A Composable and Efficient Framework for Speculative Draft Design and Training
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) generation using a lightweight draft. Existing methods evaluate complete recipes under different training configurations, leaving component effects, interactions, and composition benefits unclear. Therefore, we present LEGOSpec, a composable framework for speculative draft design and training. LEGOSpec decomposes draft models into Context, Backbone, Proposal, and Objective components that share a unified training infrastructure. Using LEGOSpec, we systematically vary components and evaluate selected combinations under matched training conditions to isolate their effects and interactions. These experiments reveal three findings: (1) Different workloads favor different backbones, depending on context length and memory budget, with within-block dependency modeling particularly important for long contexts. (2) Proposal design must balance acceptance and latency. (3) The training objective should match token distributions locally and optimize acceptance length across the block. These findings guide workload-aware configurations and DFlux, a balanced general-purpose draft combining a convolution-equipped SWA--GQA hybrid backbone, Residual Corrector, and hierarchical supervision. Across Qwen and Gemma models, DFlux improves acceptance length over the strongest baseline by up to 13.7% on regular benchmarks and 34.7% on long-context workloads. To support efficient training, LEGOSpec integrates metadata-aware scheduling and asynchronous execution, increasing training throughput by up to 79% and accelerating offline supervision preparation by up to $3.11\times$ over SpecForge.

papers.title: Modeling Bilingual Learning Through LLM Training: A Critical-Period Exploration
papers.abstract: Critical-period accounts of second-language (L2) acquisition suggest that the ability to learn a new language may depend on how easily previously acquired first-language (L1) knowledge can be modified. This exploratory computational study extends a neural language-model approach to critical-period effects by examining internal representations rather than behavior. A small two-layer GPT-2 model was trained on English and then on German (a relatively related L2) or Finnish (a relatively distant L2) through either Sequential training or Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), which limits change in parameters important for English. Mean-pooled hidden states for 20 held-out probe sentences per language were compared with those of the English-only model using cosine similarity at the embedding layer and two transformer layers after one and two L2 epochs. English similarity remained high in the transformer layers but became negative in the embedding layer. L2 similarity increased in the transformer layers, and German and Finnish differed more in the second transformer layer than in the first. EWC reduced Fisher-weighted parameter drift by about 6% but changed transformer-layer similarity by less than .001. With one training run per condition, these findings are preliminary.

papers.title: Decision-Native Multimodal Clinical Modeling via Anatomical Grounding and Confidence Calibration
papers.abstract: Structured clinical decisions from volumetric computed tomography (CT) require anatomically grounded predictions and calibrated confidence estimates. However, existing 3D medical multimodal models often suffer from uncalibrated autoregressive decoding and shortcut reliance on irrelevant anatomical regions. We introduce Radev, a decision-native multimodal model that integrates anatomy-guided visual compression, direct candidate prediction, and counterfactual confidence supervision. To bridge global context with fine-grained slice details, a frozen 3D encoder extracts reusable organ-level features, which are dynamically selected by the query to attend to 2D slice features within predicted anatomical bounds. The resulting compact visual tokens enable the language backbone to estimate candidate probabilities in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding. We further propose Counterfactual-Calibrated Training (CCT) to compare predictions under intact and intervened organ representations. CCT encourages confidence to decrease when removing target-organ evidence degrades decision quality, while penalizing excessive confidence drops under unrelated-organ removal. To facilitate rigorous evaluation, we construct CT-Verdict, a comprehensive benchmark spanning binary finding presence, multiple-choice questions, and ordinal severity assessment across both in-distribution and external cohorts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Radev significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both decision accuracy and confidence calibration, while generalizing robustly under distribution shifts. Project page at https://juntaojianggavin.github.io/projects/Radev/ .

papers.title: Positive Geometry of Oriented Matroid Strata
papers.abstract: We study the positive geometry of Grassmannians whose boundary is a union of Pl\"ucker divisors. For the full Pl\"ucker boundary the regions are closures of realization spaces of uniform oriented matroids. In rank three we show that the pair $(\mathrm{Gr}_{3,n},Z_{3,n})$ is a positive arrangement in the sense of Sturmfels and Telen for $n\le 9$ points and compute its combinatorial rank from point counts of the configuration space $\mathcal{X}_{3,n}$ over finite fields. For seven points the canonical forms of the regions span all logarithmic forms. For eight points they do not, because the M\"obius-Kantor configuration is not realizable over the reals. This determines for seven and eight points whether the integrands of Cachazo, Early and Zhang for the generalized biadjoint amplitudes of Cachazo, Early, Guevara and Mizera span the space of logarithmic forms. From ten points on, the genus is positive because a K3 surface appears in the boundary. For smaller boundaries and arbitrary rank we give a recursion that adds one point at a time and preserves the genus and the combinatorial rank. It recovers the positive Grassmannian and shows that realization spaces of stacked polytopes are regions of positive arrangements of combinatorial rank one.

papers.title: Reading Decisions Before Spans: Efficient Generative Verification
papers.abstract: A generative verifier can flag an unsupported claim before it finishes describing the error. For applications that only screen an assistant's report, the remaining generation may be unnecessary. We examine this possibility in a frozen 2B span verifier whose output chooses between an empty error list and its first object before producing any locations. Native8 stops at that choice. Prefill1 supplies the seven fixed syntax tokens that precede it and generates just the unrestricted branch token, keeping the native instruction. On 2,015 code-agent TEST responses, Prefill1 uses 84.84% less eager resident service than full generation, with released-reference F1 of 83.43 versus 83.41. It also saves 31.98% over Native8 despite identical logical token totals. This additional saving remains 6.74-26.73% under default compiled execution on the complete workload, with small changes in decisions. Evidence interventions test whether the alarm responds to the supplied facts; first-location decoding measures the additional work and localization losses when a caller also needs an error pointer.

papers.title: Increasing the Precision of IR Mapping for Incremental Data Flow Analysis
papers.abstract: Static analysis tools operate on an Intermediate Representation (IR) --- an internal model of the program on which dataflow analysis computes and stores facts against IR object identifiers. Incremental dataflow analysis reuses these cached facts across consecutive program versions, but requires an accurate mapping between IR objects in the old and new versions. When this mapping is imprecise, the consequence is not merely a missed optimization: unmapped IR objects inflate the change set, increasing the number of program points that the analyzer must recompute and forcing it to redo work that a more precise mapping would have avoided. This cost is not specific to any one kind of IR object; it arises wherever IR-level identity is unstable across versions. Any IR that decomposes nested source expressions generates temporary variables which are assigned names by a method-local counter that shifts whenever a statement is inserted or deleted earlier in the method, breaking any name- or attribute-based mapping. We present a systematic algorithm that establishes a sound, oneto-one mapping of these temporary variables across consecutive versions, and formalize and prove the soundness of the mapping, guaranteeing that every produced mapping is semantically correct. The resulting precise mapping shrinks the change set, reducing the number of program points the incremental analysis must recompute. Implemented within the Soot framework for Jimple IR and evaluated on 8 real-world Java projects with genuine edits from the BUGSWARM dataset, our approach reduces the IR change set by over 82% on average compared to Reviser's graph-differencing algorithm, while completing the full pipeline within 250 ms per project---directly countering the common assumption that a more precise change set necessarily costs more time to compute.

papers.title: Biomechanically Grounded Prediction of Selective Motor Control and Clinical Outcomes from Infant Video
papers.abstract: Early identification of cerebral palsy (CP) relies on observational assessments of spontaneous infant movement, such as the General Movement Assessment (GMA) and the Baby Observational Selective Control AppRaisal (BabyOSCAR), which require trained raters and substantial scoring time. Existing automated approaches derive hand-engineered features from two-dimensional keypoints, which describe image-plane motion rather than the three-dimensional behavior of individual joints. We present Baby Biomechanical 3D Body (BB3D), an infant-adapted, biomechanical pipeline that estimates joint-angle trajectories from single-camera video. Against a multi-view markerless motion capture reference in 17 infants, BB3D's median Procrustes-aligned error was 17.5~mm for joint centers and 20.4~mm for marker sites. A spatio-temporal transformer, pretrained on BB3D joint-angle trajectories from 1k+ single-camera recordings, and fine-tuned on 550 videos from 350 infants, predicted each individual BabyOSCAR item with a mean within-site AUC of 0.79 and the BabyOSCAR total with a Spearman correlation of 0.86 on held-out recordings. Without being trained on diagnosis, the predicted total separated infants with CP from those without CP with an AUC of 0.86, exceeding a replicated two-dimensional feature classifier (0.67) but below the expert clinician rater's total (0.97). Predicted scores also carried information about functional ability and body distribution, though less than expert clinician scores. These results show that biomechanically grounded representations of monocular video can support scalable, joint-level assessment of selective motor control in infancy

papers.title: Snap-Through Symmetry Breaking in Multicellular Aggregates
papers.abstract: Symmetry breaking is a fundamental process in biological organization. Yet the physical mechanisms that control its onset in multicellular systems remain poorly understood. Motivated by gastruloids -- multicellular aggregates in which cells differentiate and spontaneously break symmetry -- we study a two-phase viscoelastic solid drop as a minimal model of tissue polarization. We show that elastocapillary competition fundamentally alters the classical engulfing transition of fluid drops. While symmetry breaking occurs continuously in the purely viscous limit, bulk elasticity instead leads to a discontinuous snap-like transition. We demonstrate that this behavior can be understood as a wetting transition governed by a spreading coefficient which depends on the drop size and phase volume fraction. Applying our model to gastruloids, we find a critical volume fraction for symmetry breaking, providing a self-organized mechanism for robust developmental timing. Our results identify a generic elastocapillary transition that enables spontaneous symmetry breaking in biphasic drops.

papers.title: EEG-World: Context-Conditioned Dynamics of the Watching Brain
papers.abstract: Brain encoding models predict neural responses from audiovisual input, but typically overlook how ongoing brain activity shapes an individual's response. We introduce EEG-World, a recurrent world model that forecasts 10 seconds of EEG band-power dynamics from 6 seconds of preceding EEG and the subsequent audiovisual stimulus. Pretrained on continuous EEG, EEG-World learns shared neural dynamics and adapts to unseen individuals through lightweight subject-specific readouts. Using 2,584 hours of EEG from 78 participants, we show that nonlinear recurrent forecasting surpasses strong history-aware linear baselines at scale. EEG-World achieves a forecasting correlation of 0.261 versus 0.233 for the strongest history-and-video linear model, with a 3.3-second forecasting-horizon advantage. Its learned dynamics transfer to unseen participants, outperforming the linear baseline in 23 of 24 individuals after calibration. While ongoing EEG history accounts for most predictive performance, controlled stimulus analyses reveal an additional video-dependent component. This component also enables evaluation of visual representations, with V-JEPA 2 improving clip-locked prediction by 35% over combined CLIP and DINOv2 features. Our results demonstrate the value of transferable neural dynamics for individual EEG forecasting and highlight the importance of separating state-driven from stimulus-driven predictability.

papers.title: C3H: Compression-to-Consensus Criteria Hijacking in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are transforming recommender systems into content-aware decision systems. In these systems, multimodal compression and cross-modal fusion are often viewed as robustness-enhancing mechanisms against content manipulation, as compression can filter noisy signals and cross-modal consensus can suppress inconsistent anomalies. We challenge this assumption by showing that the same process can expose a compression-to-consensus (C2C) bias in ranking decisions. Signals that remain salient after compression and receive consistent support across modalities can gain disproportionate influence in candidate comparison, offering an exploitable direction for content manipulation. In this paper, we introduce C3H, a novel inference-time attack that exploits this vulnerability. Rather than relying on noisy perturbations or training-time poisoning, C3H promotes a target item by tailoring its multimodal content to align with the decision criteria implicitly expressed by the recommender. Extensive experiments demonstrate that C3H substantially increases target-item exposure while maintaining overall recommendation utility. Code is available at https://github.com/GuoweiGuan666/C3H.

papers.title: Learning World Models through Contrastive Identification of Actions
papers.abstract: Latent world models enable goal-directed planning from offline visual data, but prediction alone does not specify which action-related distinctions their representations should preserve. Inverse dynamics provides auxiliary supervision, yet squared-error action regression rewards additional information only through changes in the conditional action mean. We propose Contrastive Identification of Actions (CIA), which identifies the executed action among alternatives sampled from a history-conditioned behavior proposal. Comparing actions plausible in the same context targets information supplied by the next latent beyond history. Under exact behavior matching, we show that CIA can reward action information that leaves optimal inverse-regression error unchanged, and verify this distinction through a controlled learning example. CIA achieves higher planner-averaged mean success than the base world model and a regression inverse-dynamics baseline across five visual control benchmarks, without modifying the planner.

papers.title: An elliptic Lehmer bound of exponent one at a supersingular prime
papers.abstract: Let $E$ be an elliptic curve over a number field $K$ with good supersingular reduction at a prime $\p$. We prove that the N\'eron--Tate height of every non-torsion $P\in E(\Kbar)$ satisfies $\hh_E(P)\ge c\,D^{-1}(\log3D)^{-1}\exp(-c'\sqrt{\log3D})$, where $D=[K(x(P)):K]$ and $c,c'>0$ depend only on $E$, $K$ and $\p$; so $\hh_E(P)\ge D^{-1-o(1)}$. By a result of Elkies this applies to every elliptic curve over $\QQ$, and it improves the exponents of Masser and of Hindry and Silverman.

papers.title: Lattice models of chiral random motion: A short review
papers.abstract: Chirality, a systematic rotational bias, is ubiquitous in many random motion patterns, from bacteria cells, that swim in circles near surfaces and spinning colloids, to charged particles diffusing under the influence of magnetic fields. In two dimensions, chirality renders random transport \textit{odd}: the diffusion tensor acquires an antisymmetric part that leaves the mean-squared displacement invariant but modifies fluxes and boundary currents. Lattice models for random motion are a natural setting to study chirality, since they are exactly solvable, connect directly to heterogeneous media, cellular automata, and programmable robots, and in discrete time admit fully chiral limits with a localised bulk and edge transport. Lattice walks with a rotational bias have been introduced in different communities several times since 1960, yet without a common language or conceptual connection between them. Here we review these models from the perspective that on the lattice, chirality requires memory. Taking the recently introduced chiral random walk model as a template, we describe the walker with an internal degree of freedom. With a chiral biased updating rule, the full diffusion tensor of this chiral walker turns odd. Within this picture, we can unite persistent and chiral walks, run-and-tumble motion, and cyclic random motions in one framework. We discuss how the memory is followed into the environment; in Lorentz lattice gases, kinetic and rotor walks, and random odd environments; and into the path; in spiral self-avoiding walks.

papers.title: Parton Branching evolution in updfevolv: NNLO spacelike evolution in the ZM-VFNS and NLO timelike evolution with heavy-flavour matching
papers.abstract: We describe two extensions of the Parton Branching (PB) method as implemented in updfevolv: the next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) spacelike DGLAP evolution of parton densities in the zero-mass variable-flavour-number scheme (ZM-VFNS), and the leading and next-to-leading order (LO, NLO) timelike evolution of fragmentation functions, including the heavy-flavour matching conditions at the quark thresholds. We summarise the timelike PB formalism - momentum sum rule, Sudakov form factor, branching chain and kinematics. We give implementation details needed for the PB formalism to reproduce the semi-analytical solutions of APFEL for all flavours, including heavy quarks at threshold. This note supplements the updfevolv manual and is a technical release note for updfevolv version 2.6.0.

papers.title: Dobrowolski-type lower bounds for canonical heights of polynomials of Frobenius type
papers.abstract: Let $K$ be a number field and let $f\in\OK[x]$ be a monic polynomial of degree $d=p^r$ with $f\equiv x^d+c\pmod p$, such as $x^2+c$. We prove that every $\alpha\in\Kbar$ of degree $D$ over $K$ with infinite orbit under $f$ satisfies $$\hh_f(\alpha)\ \ge\ \frac{c_1}{D\log3D}\exp\bigl(-c_2\sqrt{\log3D}\bigr),$$ where $c_1,c_2>0$ depend only on $f$ and $K$. This implies $\hh_f(\alpha)\ge D^{-1-o(1)}$, making progress towards the dynamical Lehmer conjecture. The polynomial $f$ need not be postcritically finite. For such polynomials, for instance $x^2+1$, no lower bound of polynomial decay in $D$ was previously known. For postcritically finite polynomials such as $x^2-1$, it improves the recent quadratic bound of Habegger and Schmidt. The method is motivated by Dobrowolski's proof on Lehmer's problem.

papers.title: Testing Expansion without Connectivity via Return Probabilities
papers.abstract: We study whether every connected component of a bounded-degree graph is an edge expander, given access to its neighbor lists. Dinur and Goldreich give a tester using $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)n^\alpha$ queries for every fixed $\alpha>2/3$. We obtain \[ \widetilde O_{d,c,\beta}\!\left(\frac{n^{1/2+\beta}}{\varepsilon} +\frac{\sqrt n}{\varepsilon^4}\right) \] queries for every fixed $0 0$), each with probability at least $2/3$. No structural promise is imposed on the input. The tester compares pairwise collision probabilities at two walk lengths and starts further walks at vertices where sampled endpoints coincide. These additional samples control the contribution of vertices with larger return probabilities. We show that the resulting conditions force the longer walk to be nearly uniform on an induced expander with few edges leaving it. For fixed degree $d\ge3$ and completeness threshold $0<c<(d-2\sqrt{d-1})/2$, we show that a sufficiently small rejection expansion threshold of $\gamma d$ requires $n^{1/2+\Omega_d(\gamma)}$ queries when $\varepsilon$ is a sufficiently small multiple of $\gamma$. Thus the dependence of the excess query exponent on the rejection threshold is optimal up to constant factors in this regime. We also prove an $\Omega(\sqrt{n/\log n})$ lower bound for Cayley graphs at infinitely many input sizes.

papers.title: DiffGR00T: Execution-Aware Differentiable Training for Humanoid Whole-Body Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong results in arm-centric manipulation, yet humanoid whole-body control (WBC) requires dynamic balance and tightly coupled full-body coordination. Existing hierarchical humanoid VLAs typically decouple motion generation from physical execution, leaving tracking and balance errors unable to directly optimize the VLA generator. We propose DiffGR00T, an end-to-end differentiable training framework that couples GR00T N1.7 with SONIC, a pretrained whole-body behavior foundation model. To enable execution-aware differentiable training, we replace the non-differentiable simulator with a learned, action-conditioned world model, allowing multi-step body-execution losses to backpropagate through the frozen whole-body controller and the flow-matching sampler directly into the VLA action head. On four HumanoidArena simulation tasks, DiffGR00T improves average task success by 12.5 percentage points over the supervised base VLA (59.2% to 71.7%), demonstrating that execution-aware gradients effectively align high-level motion generation with closed-loop whole-body dynamics.

papers.title: Degree-bounded Satisfiability of Local MPNNs with Sum Aggregation is NEXPTIME-hard
papers.abstract: We prove that the following problem is NEXPTIME-hard: given a message passing neural network (MPNN) $M$ with local sum aggregation and truncated ReLU activations, and a degree bound $d$ encoded in unary, decide whether there is a pointed graph $(G,v)$ with rational node labels and degree at most $d$ that is accepted by $M$. Hardness already holds for the fixed degree bound $d=3$.

papers.title: Design, Control, and Teleoperation of a Dexterous Robotic Hand with Soft-Rigid Hybrid Fingers
papers.abstract: Adding compliance to robot hands results in higher grasp quality and robust contact with the environment. Soft hands are inherently compliant, but are typically more complex to control and model than rigid equivalents. We extend prior work on soft-rigid hybrid robot fingers into a five-fingered dexterous gripper --- an integrated tendon-driven hand that is highly compliant and controllable. Structural compliance combined with a rigid skeleton, when realized in a five-fingered hand, allow us to use linear control to achieve soft-grasping generality. We evaluate the use of this hand in a variety of teleoperated manipulation tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of the overall mechanical design and control strategy. Our contributions include: (1) Mechanical design of the a five-fingered Soft-Rigid Hybrid Hand, composed of 12 active degrees of freedom, demonstrating a high degree on generalization enabled by the soft-rigid architecture, with our gripper, able to complete 28 of the 33 (84.8\%) grasp postures in the human range. (2) Precise, high bandwidth (up to 1432deg/s extension speed, compared with 700deg/s for the equivalent human joint). (3) Position and task space controllers for the soft-rigid hybrid finger and whole hand. (4) A teleoperation framework for control of this hand, as well as demonstrations of its efficacy in a variety of grasping and manipulation tasks Further tests illustrate the hand's advantages in completing non-rigid manipulation tasks, such as picking up thin deformable objects (such as a dollar bill or folding cloth) as well as in interfacing with soft or delicate targets.

papers.title: MinPair: Measured Minimal Pairs for Fine-Grained Control in Text-to-Motion Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-motion generation has made great progress in capturing what action to perform, yet it remains limited in controlling how that action is executed. For example, when only the height word of a kick request changes, none of the tested state-of-the-art methods reaches all three of knee, waist and head height. The other words of a caption usually imply an attribute such as height, so neither the training loss nor the standard metrics require a model to use the word that states it. A model has to use this word only when it alone separates two otherwise identical captions. We introduce MinPair, which creates such caption pairs from real motion clips. It starts from rule-based motion descriptors that measure the 3D body motion of each clip. From these descriptors a language model writes MinPair captions, timed body-part captions that say how each body part moves. The same descriptors show in which attributes two clips of the same action differ. A measured minimal pair joins the true caption of one clip with an altered copy in which only one attribute takes the value measured in the other clip. A contrastive pair loss then requires a diffusion denoiser to reconstruct the clip more accurately from its true caption than from the altered copy. Training needs no synthetic motion and inference stays unchanged. Control is tested on 22 target tasks and on caption edits that each change one attribute. MinPair captions alone help motions reach their targets and improve the standard metrics M2M, R@3 and FID, yet a model trained on them still ignores most single-word edits. The pair loss raises the share of followed template edits from 11% to 60%, while the standard metrics do not improve further. With body-part captions, MinPair reaches more targets than state-of-the-art methods that were trained on up to 99 times more motion data.

papers.title: Sharp Barycentric Costs in Teichmuller Space
papers.abstract: The affine Beltrami fiber over a closed hyperbolic surface has a quadratic normal response whose least vertical $L^2$ energy equals the tangent norm dual to the hyperbolic cotangent supremum norm. We prove this calibration using a curvature identity and exact localized responses. Its strictness determines the energy measures of near-minimizers and, under an amplitude constraint, gives a positive excess with an explicit quadratic lower coefficient when the supporting differential has nondegenerate maxima. Pointwise Poincar'e barycenters of representatives in one fiber give a nonlinear realization: equal-weight pairs attain prescribed small outputs exactly, and their creation energy approaches the calibrated norm if and only if the output scale is negligible relative to the squared amplitude bound. Restoring the full local fiber graph has leading cost four times the squared Weil--Petersson norm. For degenerating surfaces, we identify the additive limit of the calibrated norm across persistent components and collar directions. The induced length metric completes to marked augmented Teichm"uller space and has distance $\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_i \ell_i + O((\sum_i \ell_i)^2)$ to a fixed pinching stratum. Systole-dependent estimates also yield exact nonlinear realizations along degenerating families.

papers.title: When Ink Meets Pixel: Intent-Aware OCR with VLMs for Human-Corrected Financial Documents
papers.abstract: Human annotations on documents (such as arrows, carets, strikethroughs, and insertions) express corrective intent yet existing OCR and document understanding systems treat these marks as visual noise rather than semantic edit operations. We introduce intent-aware OCR, the task of generating corrected transcriptions by jointly reasoning over original document content and visual intent cues (handwritten or digital) that convey edit intent. To support this setting, we present DocIntent, a multimodal dataset of 1,600 financial documents with over 5,700 annotated visual intent cues, each paired with layout-aware, intent-resolved OCR targets. We further introduce IntentBench, a 216-document benchmark designed to evaluate model robustness under diverse real-world annotation conditions. Leveraging DocIntent, we fine-tune DocIntentOCR, a suite of 3B and 7B parameter vision-language models, under direct intent supervision on corrected transcriptions. On IntentBench, the fine-tuned 3B and 7B models achieve F1-scores of 0.81 and 0.83, respectively, substantially outperforming commercial closed-source (e.g., GPT-4.1 (0.626)), and open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-3.2-Vision-90B (0.50)) demonstrating that intent-aware supervision enables compact domain-specific models to outperform substantially larger general-purpose systems on this task. This work establishes intent-aware OCR as a novel human-in-the-loop document understanding task and provides foundational resources (dataset, benchmark, models) to advance research in interactive document processing.

papers.title: Notes for a seminar on vortex layer cascades
papers.abstract: After the seminars I recently gave at New York University, the University of Chicago, Princeton University and the University of Bonn and after having been asked by some people to publish these notes, I decided to upload them to arXiv. In recent years, the method of vortex layer cascades has successfully been applied to construct finite-time singularities in multiple fluid equations (3D Euler, Boussinesq, IPM, g-SQG...). In this talk, I will motivate and describe the method and sketch how it can be applied to the 2D Boussinesq and 2D non-homogeneous Euler equations. In both systems, the growth of the vorticity is driven by an accumulated hysteresis effect triggered by the cyclic deformation of the density layers, whose dynamics is governed by an infinite chain of degenerate pendula. Our work also settles the previously open question about global existence of classical solutions of the (forced) 2D non-homogeneous Euler equations.

papers.title: Spoofing Wireless Sensing with Metasurface-based Physical Deepfakes
papers.abstract: Wireless communication networks are expanding from mere information transfer to sensing: in the Integrated Sensing and Communication paradigm, existing infrastructure and signals are reused to capture physical information about the surroundings of devices, envisioned to inform high-stakes applications such as healthcare and autonomous vehicles. From a security perspective, wireless sensing inherently trusts physical observations of the radio environment. However, as in wireless communication, the open nature of radio propagation allows attackers to tamper with victim signals. In particular, attackers can use programmable metasurfaces to manipulate wireless channels and thereby mislead sensing systems. Yet, prior metasurface-based manipulations target only individual channel features such as variance or Doppler shifts. Thus, they require knowledge of the victim sensing system and produce implausible channels that are easy to detect. In this work, we show that metasurfaces enable physically plausible manipulation of wireless sensing that is independent of the features used by the victim sensing system. Our attack reproduces genuine pre-recorded events at the physical layer and thereby synthesizes physical deepfakes of wireless channels. To this end, we develop an attack framework that controls the amplitude and phase of victim channels across time, frequency, and antennas. The key challenge here is to build a deep learning model of the interaction between metasurface and victim channel. We demonstrate that attackers can solve this challenge in several settings, e.g., by exploiting Wi-Fi Beamforming Feedback Information or replicating the victim environment. We validate the attack both in a controlled lab study on MIMO channels and with off-the-shelf Wi-Fi sensing. Our results fundamentally challenge the trustworthiness of wireless sensing.

papers.title: Boundedness and Kawamata-Viehweg vanishing for threefolds of Fano type in large characteristics
papers.abstract: We study threefolds over algebraically closed fields of large positive characteristic. Let $(X,B)$ be a projective log canonical pair with $X$ of Fano type, $-(K_X+B)$ nef and coefficients of $B$ in a fixed hyperstandard set. We obtain a monotonic complement of bounded index. For exceptional pairs the complement is Kawamata log terminal. We prove that all $\epsilon$-log canonical weak log Fano threefolds are arithmetically bounded above a characteristic threshold independent of $\epsilon$. We also prove Kawamata--Viehweg vanishing for integral $\Q$-Cartier Weil divisors on projective threefolds of Fano type above an absolute characteristic threshold.

papers.title: GOLD-SLAM: Gaussian-splatting Omnidirectional LiDAR-Depth SLAM
papers.abstract: Panoramic cameras capture nearly the entire spherical field of view in a single frame. However, the mismatch between this panoramic coverage and the field of view of LiDAR poses a substantial challenge for panoramic Gaussian splatting SLAM that relies on LiDAR depth priors. We introduce GOLD-SLAM, a Gaussian-splatting Omnidirectional LiDAR-Depth SLAM system that combines high-quality rendering with accurate geometric reconstruction. It performs tracking and mapping in the spherical domain and uses tracked visual features in regions without LiDAR coverage to improve pose estimation. To address insufficient coverage of newly observed surfaces and floating artifacts during incremental mapping, we introduce Depth-Aware Map Extension and Pruning (DAEP). To enable broader evaluation, we collect a new dataset, WHOLE, using a UAV platform across Weak-geometry, High-dynamic, Omnidirectional, Low-light, and Easy scenarios. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks and WHOLE demonstrate competitive rendering quality and improved geometric accuracy relative to perspective systems. Compared with existing panoramic baselines, GOLD-SLAM improves mean PSNR by 5.56-9.10 dB and reduces mean Depth-L1 by 71.9-83.9%. To assess deployment feasibility on resource-constrained platforms such as UAVs, we evaluate an embedded configuration of GOLD-SLAM on a Jetson Orin NX (16 GB), demonstrating online operation at the cost of reconstruction quality.

papers.title: Hadwiger\'s Covering Conjecture in Three Dimensions
papers.abstract: Let $K \subset \R^3$ be an arbitrary convex body, that is, a compact convex subset of $\R^3$ with nonempty interior. We prove unconditionally that $K$ can be covered by eight smaller positive homothetic copies of itself: there exist a scalar $\lambda \in (0, 1)$ and translation vectors $v_1, \dots, v_8 \in \R^3$ such that \[ K \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{8} (\lambda K + v_i). \] This resolves Hadwiger's covering conjecture in three dimensions. The proof works in Boltyanski's equivalent boundary illumination formulation and is completely self-contained. Parallelepipeds are covered directly by eight translates of $\frac{2}{3} K$. For any convex body $K$ that is not a parallelepiped, we place its centrally symmetric halved difference body $S = \frac{1}{2}(K - K)$ in John's position ($B^3 \subseteq S$) and show that the spherical average of its support function satisfies $8 \int_{S^2} h_S \, d\sigmatilde < 12$, with equality only for orthogonal cubes. Using outer polyhedral approximations together with Cauchy's planar perimeter formula, the full spherical measure of directions not parallel to any boundary segment of $K$, and lower semicontinuity of curve variation, we find a unit vector $w_* \in S^2$ whose shadow boundary $\Shad{K}{w_*}$ on $K$ itself is a continuous closed curve of $S$-length strictly less than $12$. Splitting $\Shad{K}{w_*}$ into six contiguous arcs of $S$-length strictly less than $2$ and applying Helly's theorem in $\R^3$ illuminates each arc with one direction, while $\pm w_*$ illuminate the remainder of $\partial K$. The proof was discovered using an experimental harness on top of Gemini~4 Carbon and formally verified in Lean~4.

papers.title: ASTERISM: Do Multimodal LLMs Actually Look at All the Images?
papers.abstract: Multi-image benchmarks aim to test whether a multimodal large language model (MLLM) combines evidence across images, but many of their items can be answered from a single image. Across about 33k items from 19 public benchmarks, our audit and a two-stage single-image filter find that one image or the question alone settles 24.2% of them. On these items, MLLMs recover from one image a median 78% of the accuracy that all images add over the text alone, so these items reward answering from one image, which we call the single-image shortcut. MLLMs take this shortcut even on items where one image is not enough. On such items, most of their wrong answers repeat an answer they give from one image, at a rate well above chance. We build ASTERISM, to our knowledge the largest audited multi-image benchmark, from these 19 benchmarks by keeping their items that need more than one image. Its 18.7k items, 2.0k of them corrected or rewritten, share one format, one scorer and seven task categories. We also release ASTERISM-Train with 49k training items and ASTERISM-Lite, a hard subset whose items we manually verify one by one. On ASTERISM-Lite, the strongest proprietary MLLM scores 68%. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), now common in MLLM post-training, rewards the shortcut as well, because a correct answer read off one image earns as much reward as one that combines images. In line with this, existing RLVR objectives add little to the ASTERISM score. To stop rewarding the shortcut in training as ASTERISM does in evaluation, we propose cross-image credit assignment (CICA), an extension of RLVR that moves the credit toward the tokens that need more than one image. On three open-source MLLMs, CICA raises the ASTERISM score by 2.6 to 6.0 points, more than twice the gain of each general and vision-specific RL objective trained on the same data.

papers.title: SynAVID: A Synthetic Audio-Visual Immersive Dataset of Dynamic Scenes
papers.abstract: Immersive scene modeling requires synchronized visual and auditory observations under changing viewpoints and scene conditions. Obtaining such observations and references for controlled scene changes remains challenging. We introduce SynAVID, a synthetic audio-visual immersive dataset comprising eight indoor and outdoor scenes. Each minute-scale episode combines fixed camera arrays and moving trajectories with synchronized, viewpoint-dependent binaural audio. Shared scene dynamics, sound-source events, and observer poses drive visual rendering and geometry-aware acoustic synthesis. We evaluate existing methods for visual reconstruction, binaural audio reconstruction, and audiovisual editing. Mixed-observation configurations generally improve visual reconstruction on fixed and moving test views, while transiently occupied and sparsely observed regions remain challenging. Methods rank differently on spectral, interaural, and perceptual audio metrics. Geometric and instance annotations expose uneven observation support and local Gaussian representations beyond aggregate scores. Paired references assess target edits and surrounding content, while controlled geometry changes produce listener-dependent acoustic responses. The project page is available at https://avery-xu.github.io/synavid-project/.

papers.title: MaskedVGGT: Masked Multi-View Transformers Are Scalable 3D Learners
papers.abstract: Multi-view feed-forward models show strong scalability, but their reliance on costly geometric annotations limits data scaling. Existing 3D self-supervised approaches reduce this reliance through cross-view completion (e.g., CroCo, MuM, Muskie) or novel-view synthesis (e.g., RayZer, E-RayZer), typically learning image representations and cross-view interactions jointly. We argue that learning single image representations from scratch is unnecessary for 3D pretraining methods, as doing so fails to benefit from the continuing advances in 2D foundation models (e.g., DINO, CLIP, frontier VLMs). We introduce MaskedVGGT, which freezes a strong pretrained 2D encoder and pretrains only an added, randomly initialized multi-view transformer, focusing on learning interactions across views. MaskedVGGT pretrains the multi-view transformer through masked self-distillation without annotations: a student predicts targets at masked locations based on complete anchor views and heavily masked remaining views, while an exponential-moving-average teacher provides prediction targets based on unmasked inputs. In experiments across model sizes up to 1B parameters, MaskedVGGT pretraining followed by fine-tuning outperforms single-stage supervised VGGT-$\Omega$ training with the same training data, model architecture, and total number of optimization updates. MaskedVGGT also outperforms E-RayZer, CroCo, MuM, and Muskie, providing evidence for the effectiveness of building multi-view pretraining on strong 2D representations. Finally, extending pretraining with additional unlabeled videos further improves generalization, and the learned representations transfer to diverse downstream tasks. These results demonstrate an effective division of learning: reuse strong image representations from 2D pretraining and learn cross-view interactions from unlabeled multi-view data without relying on geometric annotations.

papers.title: Trading BRAM for LUTs: Hybrid Bit-Level Weight Storage for FPGA-Based Spiking Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer an attractive paradigm for energy-efficient AI inference, while their deployment on reconfigurable hardware enables application-specific acceleration without sacrificing model reprogrammability. However, realizing this potential on FPGAs is often severely constrained by the immense on-chip memory needed to store synaptic weights. Existing compression techniques reduce this storage requirement at the cost of weight precision or accuracy. This work presents a hybrid bit-level weight-storage scheme that trades BRAM capacity for FPGA logic resources while preserving the original weights unmodified. Selected weight bits are implemented using Look-Up Tables (LUTs), while the remaining bits are stored in BRAM and jointly reconstructed during inference. We integrate this approach into a spatial dataflow SNN architecture and introduce a practical bit-mapping heuristic that efficiently partitions weight bits between BRAM and LUT-based logic without modifying the weights. Experimental evaluation demonstrates more than 26% reduction in BRAM utilization with a modest increase in LUT and register usage, resulting in significant overall power savings.

papers.title: Hochschild operations and other invariants of stable equivalences of Morita type
papers.abstract: We study stable equivalences defined by bimodule tensor identities over a commutative ring $R$. For the $R$-split exact structure, these identities preserve positive Hochschild homology and positive Hochschild cohomology with its cup product, Gerstenhaber bracket and, in prime characteristic, restricted power. A triangular comparison also identifies the relative singular Hochschild cochain complexes as $B_\infty$-algebras. For reduced pairs of finite-dimensional Frobenius algebras over an algebraically closed field, with diagonalizable Nakayama automorphisms, we construct compatible Frobenius functionals and compare the Tate--Hochschild BV operators in all degrees. For flat algebras over $R$ we give a Hochschild-cohomological criterion for comparing marked associative deformations. It applies to biadjoint Morita-type pairs and, by reduction, to all stable equivalences of Morita type between finite-dimensional algebras over any field.
